# discussion

Practice repo - vishpala-decisions

UC repo - uc-automa

**Cross-cutting decisions belong in one central repository.** These are decisions that govern several repositories or the whole practice: licensing, documentation conventions, metadata and front matter, citation style, versioning, and SAT architecture. Spread across repositories, there's no obvious home for them, no single numbering scheme, and no way to see what is currently in force. Centralizing them gives you one index, one history and one place to send a client who asks why you do things a certain way.

**Component-local decisions are better kept next to the code they govern.** These are choices that only make sense inside one tool, such as why `uc-radar` stores scores a certain way. Kept beside the code, they get updated in the same commit when the code changes. Moved away, they drift out of sync.

This split also fits your sovereignty principle and SAT's goal of liberating a collection from one instance and moving it to another. If a component is handed to a client or forked, its local decisions should travel with it. A component that depends on a central repository to explain itself is a small form of lock-in.

**What I'd suggest**

- **Make the central repository practice-level, not Universal Cake-level.** Your cross-cutting decisions span SAT, sat-doc-automa and Universal Cake, so uc-automa is too narrow a home. A name like `vishpala-decisions`, or simply `decisions`, under steelcj would work. uc-automa can then hold Universal Cake-specific decisions or link to the central ones.
- **Have the central repository index everything, including local records.** An automation step can scan each repository for decision-record front matter and build one index, published as an Eleventy site. You get a single view without moving the local records.
- **Give every record a stable identifier.** Use your `urn:uuid:` values plus a readable ID with a domain prefix, such as `LIC-0001` or `SAT-0003`, so records from different repositories never collide. References then survive moves.
- **Use explicit statuses: proposed, accepted, superseded and deprecated.** Your two SAT ADRs that rest on assumptions that no longer hold are the clearest case. Mark them superseded with a link to whatever replaces them, rather than deleting them, so the reasoning trail stays intact.
- **Move records without breaking links.** When you move a record, leave a short stub at the old path pointing to its new home, and keep the git history. Record the consolidation itself as the first decision in the new repository.

**What to put where now**

- **Central repository:** the licensing decision, the trademark policy, house markdown style, front matter and metadata conventions, the SAT config cascade and its role structure, and the ADRs on naming parity and identifiers.
- **Stays local, indexed centrally:** implementation decisions inside a single tool or site.
- **Not a decision record:** the migration checklist. It's a work plan, so it belongs in uc-automa next to the work, with a link from the licensing decision.

I can draft the README and folder layout for the central repository, a decision-record template with the front matter and status fields, or the first record covering this consolidation.  === en-ca/projects/licence-migration/index.md

Status: Planned.

## Before changing anything

- [ ] Check third-party content (images, fonts, quoted text) in the documentation and record its licence.

## Code repositories

- [ ] Replace `LICENSE` with the MIT License text, naming the copyright holder and year.

- [ ] Update package metadata (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml` or equivalent) to `MIT`.
- [ ] Add a `NOTICE` or README section stating that releases up to the tagged AGPL release remain AGPL-3.0-or-later.

- [ ] Update the licence-statement convention in `sat-doc-automa` so new documents default to CC BY 4.0.

- [ ] Mark trademarks in licence notices as excluded from the licence, for example "Universal Cake and its logo are not covered by this licence".

## Name and marks

- [ ] Publish the [trademark policy](../../policies/trademark-policy.md) alongside the first MIT release.
- [ ] Link the trademark policy from every README and from the radar site footer.
- [ ] Decide whether to register the Universal Cake name with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office.

## Communication

- [ ] Record the completed migration in the LIC-0001 changelog.

# Universal Cake trademark policy

You may use Universal Cake code and content freely under their licences, but only the official project may use the Universal Cake name and logo to identify a product, service, evaluation or radar.

Status: provisional, pending confirmation by the maintainer.

## Why this policy exists

Universal Cake code is licensed under MIT and its content under CC BY 4.0, so anyone can copy, change and republish it. Neither licence covers the name or logo. This policy keeps the name meaningful: when people see "Universal Cake", they should know the work came from the project and was scored against the published Evaluation Metrics.

## What the marks are

- The name "Universal Cake", and close variants such as "UniversalCake" and "UC Radar".
- The Universal Cake logo and icons.
- Any other name or design the project identifies as a mark on its official site.

## Uses that need no permission

- Saying that your work is based on, uses or is compatible with Universal Cake, for example "built on Universal Cake tools" or "scored with the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics, version 2.0".
- Redistributing unmodified official releases under their original names.
- Writing about, reviewing, teaching or criticizing Universal Cake.
- Linking to the official project with its name or logo.
- Quoting an official radar evaluation unchanged, with credit and a link.

## Uses that need permission

- Naming a fork, product, service or company "Universal Cake" or anything confusingly similar.
- Using the logo on modified tools, a hosted service or merchandise.
- Presenting a modified or independent evaluation as an official Universal Cake evaluation or placement on the official radar.
- Implying that the project or Vishpala endorses, certifies or partners with you.
- Using the marks in domain names, social media handles or app names.

## If you modify the work

- Give your version its own name.
- Say what you changed and which official version you started from, as CC BY 4.0 already requires for content.
- Keep the original copyright and licence notices, as MIT requires for code.
- Make clear that your version is not the official project.

## Official sources

Official Universal Cake releases and evaluations are published at [github.com/steelcj](https://github.com/steelcj). Anything published elsewhere under the name should link back there.

## Asking for permission

Requests to use the marks in ways not covered above can be sent to the maintainer through the official repository. The project intends to say yes to uses that help people, especially non-profit, educational and accessibility work, as long as the use is not confusing.

## Licence of this policy

This policy covers trademarks only. It does not change the MIT or CC BY 4.0 licences on Universal Cake code and content, and those licences do not grant trademark rights.

This policy is not legal advice. It should be reviewed by a lawyer familiar with Canadian trademark law before it is relied on.

# Moving Universal Cake Tools to GPL-2.0

10 Oct 2026 · @sirhc

## Summary

Moving the Universal Cake tools from AGPL-3.0-or-later to GPL-2.0 would make them easier for cautious organizations to adopt, but it would remove the protection that matters most for a hosted radar: the right of network users to get the source. GPL-2.0 also lacks an explicit patent grant, is not compatible with Apache-2.0 code, and breaks the CC BY-SA 4.0 bridge that runs only to GPLv3.

The draft conclusion is to keep AGPL-3.0-or-later for anything run as a service, and to consider GPL-3.0-or-later, not GPL-2.0, for tools that are only ever distributed and run locally. This stays provisional until the licensing owner confirms it.

## What would change

The biggest difference is the network clause; most of the others follow from GPLv3 being written 16 years after GPLv2.

| Term                                                         | AGPL-3.0-or-later (current)   | GPL-2.0-only           | GPL-2.0-or-later        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Published                                                    | 2007                          | 1991                   | 1991                    |
| Source owed to network users of a modified version           | Yes, section 13               | No                     | No                      |
| Source owed when copies are distributed                      | Yes                           | Yes                    | Yes                     |
| Explicit patent licence from contributors                    | Yes                           | No, implied at best    | No, implied at best     |
| Anti-tivoization (installation information for consumer devices) | Yes                           | No                     | No                      |
| Cure period after a violation                                | Yes, 30 and 60 day provisions | No, rights end at once | No, rights end at once  |
| Can move to a future licence version                         | Yes                           | No                     | Yes, to GPLv3 and later |
| Combinable with GPLv3 or AGPLv3 code                         | Yes                           | No                     | Yes, by choosing v3     |
| Combinable with Apache-2.0 code                              | Yes                           | No, in the FSF's view  | Yes, by choosing v3     |

## Advantages of GPL-2.0

The case for GPL-2.0 is mostly about adoption and simplicity, not stronger protection.

- Fewer policy blocks. Many companies and some public bodies ban AGPL code outright but allow GPL-2.0, so procurement and IT reviews get shorter.
- Lighter duties for clients who host. A municipality or NGO that modifies a tool and runs it internally or on a public site would owe source only if it distributed copies, not to every visitor.
- Familiarity. GPL-2.0 is the licence of the Linux kernel and has decades of case history and community practice behind it.
- Shorter text. GPL-2.0 is about half the length of AGPLv3 and easier to explain to a non-specialist client.
- Fixed terms (GPL-2.0-only). No future licence version can change what contributors agreed to, which is the reason Linus Torvalds keeps the kernel on version 2 only.
- Kernel and embedded alignment. Code that might one day be shared with GPL-2.0-only projects, such as kernel modules or some embedded firmware, can be combined directly.

## Disadvantages of GPL-2.0

The main cost is that a hosted fork could stay closed, which is the exact risk the AGPL was chosen to prevent.

- The network gap. A vendor or consultancy could modify `uc-radar`, run it as a paid rating service and never publish its changes. GPL-2.0 is triggered by distributing copies, not by serving users.
- No explicit patent grant. Contributors do not expressly licence their patents, and there is no patent retaliation clause, so downstream users of a tool have weaker protection.
- Harsh termination. Any violation ends a licensee's rights immediately, with no cure period, which is a poor fit for small organizations that make honest mistakes.
- No anti-tivoization. A device maker could ship a modified tool on locked hardware that users cannot update, which works against agency and longevity.
- Compatibility losses. GPL-2.0-only cannot be combined with GPLv3, AGPLv3 or Apache-2.0 code, which rules out a large share of modern libraries (Apache Software Foundation, n.d.).
- Dated wording. GPLv2 was written around US concepts like "distribution"; GPLv3 uses "convey" and "propagate" to work more evenly across jurisdictions, including Canada.
- Mixed signals. A practice that scores vendors on sovereignty would be choosing a weaker copyleft for its own hosted tools.

result.output: /home/initial/areas/buisness-ideas: total 4 -rw-rw-r-- 1 initial initial 47 Oct 19 01:21 httpswww.facebook.comreel28036421662727524.md /home/initial/areas/saas: total 16 -rw-rw-r-- 1 initial initial 8416 Oct 15 17:25 how-much-does-the-city-of-montreal-spend-on-saas.md -rw-rw-r-- 1 initial initial 3115 Oct 15 17:20 canada-software-as-a-service-saas-market-highlights.md /home/initial/areas/clients: total 4 drwxrwxr-x 2 initial initial 4096 Oct 15 16:22 francois --- title: "Creating the Initial osat-manager-git: Process Overview" description: "How the initial osat-manager-git was scoped and planned: from feasibility to a unified git base, Universal Cake requirements, and a proposed build sequence." identifier: "urn:uuid:90391798-a7d9-4f30-b7c1-bd9e40bba160" language: "en-ca" creator: "Christopher Steel" date: "2026-09-30" version: "0.1.0" status: "provisional" relation: "https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar" --- # Creating the Initial osat-manager-git: Process Overview osat-manager-git is being built first as a unified git base: it manages multiple git installations on Linux, macOS and Windows through the standard osat CLI, with translated messages, so that every other osat manager can rely on git being present and correct. This overview records how that decision was reached and how the work proceeds. It is a provisional draft, drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), and stays provisional until Christopher Steel confirms it. ## Where this fits The long-term goal is highly accessible, safe, secure and multilingual applications, measured against the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics (Steel, n.d.). One example is a very user-friendly, git-backed interface for managing SAT content, where a person adds a document, gives it a good title and description, and never needs to learn git. That interface depends on git working the same way everywhere. osat-manager-git provides that foundation, and building it is also the first chance to turn the Universal Cake metrics into concrete, testable requirements. ## Step one: confirm feasibility Two meanings of "managing git" were considered: managing git itself, and managing repositories inside a SAT hierarchy. Both are feasible. Managing git itself came first, because the repository work depends on it and because the SAT config cascade specification is still being written. ## Step two: define a baseline contract, not an install method The central idea is a baseline contract that says what "git is ready" means: - a minimum git version; - the capabilities other osat managers rely on; - required configuration, such as line endings, `safe.directory`, credential helper, and long paths on Windows. Other managers ask osat-manager-git whether the contract is met, rather than probing git themselves. How git gets installed matters less than whether the contract holds. ## Step three: set the scope The first plan was a thin check-only stub. That changed: the full manager is needed in the short term, because other osat managers need git soon. The agreed scope is: - manage multiple git installations per machine, not just one; - run on Linux, macOS and Windows; - follow the standard osat CLI defined by the osat-manager specification; - provide translated messages, starting with en-ca and fr-ca. Where the osat-manager specification defines commands, output or translation format, the specification takes precedence over this project's own documents. ## Step four: write Universal Cake requirements through a worked example General metrics become useful only when a real task forces them into testable statements. The chosen task is "Add a document" to SAT content, done end to end: 1. The interface asks osat-manager-git whether the baseline is met, and explains any problem in plain language. 2. The person fills in title, description and language. 3. The tool writes a markdown file with Dublin Core front matter and a `urn:uuid:` identifier. 4. The tool records the change in git with a generated message. 5. The person sees "Saved" and a readable history, and can undo with "Remove this change". Each requirement gets an ID, one statement, and a test with a clear pass or fail. They fall into five areas. | Area | Prefix | What it secures | | --- | --- | --- | | Inclusive design | ID | WCAG 2.2 level AA (World Wide Web Consortium [W3C], 2023), keyboard and screen-reader use, plain language, no git terms. | | Multilingual | ML | All strings from a message catalog; en-ca and fr-ca language tags (Phillips & Davis, 2009); git's own output never shown directly. | | Security | SEC | No shell, `--end-of-options` before user input (Git Project, n.d.), safe file names, localhost only, hooks off by default (OWASP Foundation, n.d.). | | Agency and longevity | AL | Plain markdown in standard git, full history, undo, export, no network dependency. | | osat-manager-git | GIT | Discovery, install and removal, active installation per scope, baseline checks, osat CLI conformance, translations, idempotence, signed sources. | These requirements are recorded in the companion document, *Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice*. ## Design principles carried forward These principles came out of the feasibility work and guide later projects, including the web interface. - **The git CLI is the engine.** Parsing git's machine-readable porcelain output gives access to all of git. Libraries such as libgit2 or isomorphic-git are used only where they clearly help, because they do not cover all of git. - **Progressive disclosure.** Common tasks get excellent guided flows; advanced operations stay reachable but out of the way. - **Security from day one.** A service that runs git is attack surface: each repository is sandboxed, and hooks from untrusted repositories are treated as code execution. - **Translate meaning, not git.** Structured results map to the project's own message catalog, so every language gets the same clarity. - **Hardest accessibility first.** Diffs and merge conflicts are the hardest things to make screen-reader friendly, so they are prototyped early. ## Proposed build sequence This order is proposed, not yet confirmed. 1. Write the baseline contract as one versioned file. 2. Build discovery: list every git installation with version, path and origin. 3. Build check: report each installation against the baseline as JSON, following the osat CLI. 4. Build install, upgrade and remove through each platform's native route: apt, dnf, Homebrew and winget. 5. Build active-installation switching per machine and per user. 6. Complete the en-ca and fr-ca catalogs, and test on Linux Mint, Fedora, macOS and Windows 11. 7. Build the Add Document slice on top, and test it against the Universal Cake requirements. ## Before building an interface: evaluate prior art GitHub Desktop, GitButler and Forgejo should be evaluated against the Universal Cake metrics first. The results show which gaps in accessibility, language support and safety a new interface would actually fill. ## Open questions - Which shared commands, output schema and exit codes does the osat-manager specification define? - Which minimum git version does the baseline set? - Can the active installation also be set per SAT node, through the config cascade? - Which Dublin Core and `sat:` fields does the Add Document form collect? - Which languages follow en-ca and fr-ca? - Which license applies to this document? ## Changelog | Date | Version | Change | | --- | --- | --- | | 2026-09-30 | 0.1.0 (provisional) | First draft of the process overview. | ## References Git Project. (n.d.). *gitcli: Git command-line interface and conventions*. Git documentation. https://git-scm.com/docs/gitcli [Return to text](#cite-git-nd-1) OWASP Foundation. (n.d.). *OS command injection defense cheat sheet*. OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html [Return to text](#cite-owasp-nd-1) Phillips, A., & Davis, M. (2009). *Tags for identifying languages* (BCP 47, RFC 5646). Internet Engineering Task Force. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC5646 [Return to text](#cite-phillips-2009-1) Steel, C. (n.d.). *Universal Cake evaluation metrics* [Unpublished manuscript, uc-radar repository]. GitHub. https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar [Return to text](#cite-steel-nd-1) World Wide Web Consortium. (2023). *Web content accessibility guidelines (WCAG) 2.2* (W3C Recommendation). https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ [Return to text](#cite-w3c-2023-1) --- title: "Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice" description: "Testable Universal Cake requirements for osat-manager-git and a git-backed Add Document interface for SAT content." identifier: "urn:uuid:82642c55-a2c5-4800-9f24-600400f9e195" language: "en-ca" creator: "Christopher Steel" date: "2026-09-30" version: "0.1.0" status: "provisional" relation: "https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar" --- # Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice This is a provisional draft. The version stays provisional until Christopher Steel confirms it. It was drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic). ## Purpose and scope This document turns the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics (Steel, n.d.) into testable requirements, using one real task as the worked example: adding a document to SAT content through a friendly, git-backed interface. Every later project, including a full SAT content interface, inherits these requirements rather than starting from zero. Two components are in scope: - **osat-manager-git**, in full: it manages multiple git installations per machine on Linux, macOS and Windows, through the standard osat CLI with translated messages. Other osat managers depend on it. - **The Add Document slice**: a small local web interface that writes one document into SAT content and records it in git, without the person needing to know git. The config cascade resolver is not in scope. The slice uses one fixed content location until the cascade specification is settled. ## The worked example: Add a document

Today it also lists untracked files git does not ignore, so a draft left in a checkout lands in the generated index; on 2026-10-11 it picked up two untracked session notes. - A decision on how a decision's version changes after it is accepted: uc-automa 0029 covers directives only, and 0030's open question was answered in place on 2026-10-11 with its version left at 0.1.0. - In 0.3.0: migrate sat-doc-automa's style rules into directives, one rule per file, each with a check where one is possible: commas rather than em dashes, no horizontal rules, no hard wraps, Citation Anchor Pairs. - Verify end to end on macOS and Windows; uc-automa reaches 1.0.0 only when all three platforms are verified. - `uc-automa docs fetch`, checking out the pinned version's documentation into the per-user data directory. - A compatibility range for `automa_version`, to be reconsidered at 1.0.0. - Publish uc-portage and uc-automa somewhere pip can install them from, so the pre-commit hook can install itself. --- title: "Decision: Pilot Manager restic" dc:title: "Decision: Pilot Manager restic" dc:creator: "Christopher Steel" dc:contributor: "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), AI assistance" dc:subject: "OSAT manager, restic, pilot, D18" dc:description: "The pilot OSAT manager is restic, as osat-manager-restic, succeeding osat-fluent-restic-tool." dc:date: "2026-10-09" dc:type: "Text" dc:format: "text/markdown" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:d23f6735-0dc3-4a96-ac2d-f1ce7b22aea3" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" sat:version: "0.1.0" sat:status: "Accepted" sat:decision: "D18" --- # Decision: Pilot Manager restic Version: 0.1.0 Status: Accepted ## Context The osat-manager process needed a first repository built entirely by the new approach, to test both the tooling and the process itself. (2026b). *Brief: uc-automa foundation* (Version 0.1.0) [Unpublished manuscript]. urn:uuid:965f6290-3d72-4631-ad66-9b4c6f63db96 [↩](#cite-steel-2026b) ## Changelog | Version | Date | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Initial version | ## License This document, *Decision: Pilot Manager restic*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). --- title: "Decision: Shared Manager Package" dc:title: "Decision: Shared Manager Package" dc:creator: "Christopher Steel" dc:contributor: "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), AI assistance" dc:subject: "OSAT managers, shared package, OpenPGP, YAML, resolver" dc:description: "Behaviour every OSAT manager shares lives in one installed, standard-library-only package that each manager depends on; the YAML subset reader, the data lookup and the OpenPGP verifier move there in 0.2.0." dc:date: "2026-10-09" dc:type: "Text" dc:format: "text/markdown" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:2ecde9ee-b7bb-4d51-b58b-f0ca6bc4fc85" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" sat:version: "0.1.0" sat:status: "Accepted" --- # Decision: Shared Manager Package Version: 0.1.0 Status: Accepted ## Context The OSAT manager process left open whether shared manager behaviour should live in one installed package that every manager depends on. result.output: uc-automa/CHANGELOG.md uc-automa/en-ca/docs/sessions/2026-10-09--uc-automa-foundation-v0.1.0.md uc-automa/en-ca/docs/decisions/0022--sidecar-named-for-the-repository-v0.1.0.md uc-automa/en-ca/docs/decisions/0018--pilot-manager-restic-v0.1.0.md uc-automa/en-ca/docs/decisions/0024--shared-manager-package-v0.1.0.md uc-automa/en-ca/docs/decisions/0023--init-writes-the-repository-configuration-v0.1.0.md uc-automa/en-ca/docs/decisions/0026--release-ceremony-v0.1.0.md 2026-10-09--uc-automa-foundation/README.md 2026-10-09--uc-automa-foundation/CLAUDE.md 2026-10-09--uc-automa-foundation/brief/brief--uc-automa-foundation-v0.1.0.md --- title: "Decision: Build manage-restic" dc:title: "Decision: Build manage-restic" dc:creator: "Christopher Steel" dc:contributor: "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), AI assistance" dc:subject: "OSAT manager, restic, verification, OpenPGP, manager.yaml, platforms" dc:description: "Build manage-restic as the pilot OSAT manager for restic: the platforms targeted, two-step verification against a pinned signing key in the standard library, and where it differs from the contract and the process." dc:date: "2026-10-09" dc:type: "Text" dc:format: "text/markdown" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:1ede50fa-cf0c-48d5-b121-1506673c2b9f" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" sat:version: "0.1.0" sat:status: "Accepted" --- # Decision: Build manage-restic Version: 0.1.0 Status: Accepted ## Context Every OSAT manager starts with a decision record naming the managed tool, its radar entry, the platforms targeted first, and anything the manager does differently from the contract [(Steel, 2026a)](#ref-steel-2026a). restic was chosen as the pilot manager by uc-automa 0018, succeeding osat-fluent-restic-tool. Its radar entry, *uc-radar: restic, Backup Tool*, version 0.1.0, is a draft awaiting placement in uc-radar. restic publishes, for each release, one compressed binary per platform, `restic___.bz2` for Linux and macOS and `.zip` for Windows, a `SHA256SUMS` file, and a detached OpenPGP signature of it, `SHA256SUMS.asc`, made with Alexander Neumann's RSA key `CF8F 18F2 8445 7597 3F79 D4E1 91A6 868B D3F7 A907` [(restic authors, n.d.)](#ref-restic-nd). ## Decision Build `manage-restic`, meeting the OSAT manager contract, with these choices: - **Platforms targeted first:** Linux on amd64 and arm64, macOS on amd64 and arm64, Windows on amd64. Only Linux on amd64 is verified for 0.1.0. - **Verification:** every download is checked in two steps before it is unpacked. The signature on `SHA256SUMS` is verified against the key pinned in `manager.yaml`, by fingerprint; then the asset's SHA-256 is compared with the signed list. The extracted binary must then report the requested version before it is placed. - **Signature verification in the standard library:** the process requires the standard library only, with no shell commands, and Windows rarely has `gpg`. The manager therefore verifies the RSA signature itself, implementing the parts of RFC 4880 it needs and refusing the rest. osat-fluent-restic-tool had deferred signature checking for exactly this reason. - **Strict verification rules:** the hash is exactly SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512; the signature's hashed area names the pinned fingerprint as issuer, and an issuer only in the unhashed area, or none, fails; every issuer named must be the pinned key; the 16-bit hash prefix must match; the PKCS#1 v1.5 encoding is compared byte for byte; and malformed or truncated input fails closed. Where these are stricter than `gpg`, the test vectors name the rule. - **Pin the key that actually signs:** the pinned fingerprint names the key that makes the signatures, by its own fingerprint, whether a primary key or a subkey. restic signs with its primary key, `CF8F 18F2 8445 7597 3F79 D4E1 91A6 868B D3F7 A907`. A subkey's binding to its primary is not checked; pinning the subkey's own fingerprint is the trust decision. - **Independent review:** because the verifier is security-critical, new code, it is reviewed independently, by a reviewer who did not see it written, before osat-manager-restic is tagged, and again after any rewrite. Every test vector's expected verdict is confirmed with `gpg --verify`. - **Reading manager.yaml without PyYAML:** the manager must run on the Python manage-python installs, which has no PyYAML, so it reads the strict subset of YAML that `manager.yaml` uses and refuses anything else. This conflicts with the process's own pairing of a YAML manifest with standard-library-only code, and is recorded as a finding about the process. - **Finding manager.yaml:** the manager follows uc-automa 0019, mapping `manager.yaml` into the package and falling back to a proven checkout, but with its own small lookup rather than uc-portage's resolver, since uc-portage is not standard-library-only. This is a second copy of that rule, to be retired if the shared manager package becomes real. - **The verified archive** keeps the downloaded asset with the `SHA256SUMS` and signature that verified it, so an offline restore re-checks both. - **Install and activate together:** `--install` makes the installed version active, because osat-fluent-restic-tool's install that did not activate was misleading. - **Locations:** the install root is `osat/restic` in each platform's per-user data directory, as the process proposes, while whether `osat` is the right name remains open. Launchers go to `~/.local/bin` on Linux and macOS and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\osat\bin` on Windows, which the user adds to `PATH`. - **Nothing left behind:** the manager records each directory it creates outside its install root and removes it on uninstall if it is empty. ## Consequences - The pinned key changes only by a new version of `manager.yaml`, reviewed like any other change. - The manager never touches restic's own configuration, cache, repositories or passwords, and does not use `restic self-update`. - Reaching 1.0.0 needs macOS and Windows verified (uc-automa 0011). ## References restic authors. (n.d.). *Installation*. restic documentation. Retrieved October 9, 2026, from https://restic.readthedocs.io/en/stable/020_installation.html [↩](#cite-restic-nd) Steel, C. result.output: --- title: "Creating an OSAT Manager Repository" dc:title: "Creating an OSAT Manager Repository" dc:creator: "Christopher Steel" dc:contributor: "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), AI assistance" dc:subject: "OSAT managers, repository creation, uc-automa, offerings, cross-platform testing, release" dc:description: "The process for creating a new osat-manager repository with uc-automa, from radar assessment to first release, in ten stages with gates." dc:date: "2026-10-11" dc:type: "Text" dc:format: "text/markdown" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:b18e2ed3-b364-4880-b3c7-5676961f0174" dc:source: "Hand-off package 2026-10-09--uc-automa-foundation, inputs/revise/osat-manager--creating-a-new-repository-v0.1.0.md, not under version control" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" sat:version: "0.4.0" sat:status: "Accepted" --- # Creating an OSAT Manager Repository Version: 0.4.0 Status: Accepted ## Summary A new OSAT manager goes through ten stages, from a radar assessment of the tool it manages to its first release, and each stage ends at a checkable gate. The repository is created fresh, receives everything shared by subscribing to uc-automa's offerings, and copies nothing by hand. Its layout type is `osat-manager`, described in the directory guide [(Steel, 2026a)](#ref-steel-2026a). ## What an OSAT manager is An OSAT manager is a governed tool that installs another tool into user space and manages its versions there, with no elevated privilege, no system package manager and no compiler. The contract below is drawn from osat-manager-python, the first manager, which installs self-contained CPython runtimes and runs as `manage-python` [(Steel, 2026c)](#ref-steel-2026c). Every manager meets the same contract, so a person who has used one can use them all. | Capability | What it means | | --- | --- | | User-space install | Installs into the user's own directories; never needs administrator rights | | Versions side by side | Several versions of the managed tool can be installed at once | | Switching | One command makes a chosen version the active one | | Aliases | A generic alias, such as `restic`, beside versioned ones, such as `restic-0.18`; any alias can be renamed | | Protection | Installed versions are guarded against accidental modification | | Nothing left behind | Uninstalling removes everything the manager owns, and a parent directory such as `~/.local/bin` only if the manager created it and it is now empty; a directory that holds anything else is never removed | | Verified archive | Every download is verified before it is unpacked, and kept with the checksums and signature that verified it, so a version can be restored offline and re-checked | | Self-install | The manager installs itself, so it works from any directory | | Three platforms | Linux, macOS and Windows, with each platform's status stated honestly | ## Naming | Thing | Pattern | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Repository | `osat-manager-` | `osat-manager-restic` | | Command | `manage-` | `manage-restic` | | Python package | `osat_manager_` | `osat_manager_restic` | | SAT sidecar | `.osat-manager-.assets/` | `.osat-manager-restic.assets/` | | Documents before 1.0.0 | `-vX.Y.Z.md` | `using-manage-restic-v0.1.0.md` | | Documents from 1.0.0 | `.md` | `using-manage-restic.md` | `` is the managed tool's own name in lowercase, with hyphens for any spaces. The Python package uses underscores, because Python cannot import hyphens; everything else uses hyphens. ## Repository layout The `osat-manager` layout extends `python-tool`, which extends `base`. `uc-automa check` compares the repository with it. ```text osat-manager-/ ├── README.md what it manages, install, platform status table ├── LICENSE from license-mit ├── LICENSES/ from the licence offerings ├── REUSE.toml seeded by reuse ├── CHANGELOG.md seeded by changelog ├── VERSION seeded by version-file ├── ROADMAP.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── CLAUDE.md ends with the claude-signpost block ├── .uc-automa.yaml written once by uc-automa init ├── .uc-portage-state.yaml written by uc-automa offerings apply ├── .osat-manager-.assets/ │ ├── archive.yaml │ └── dc.yaml ├── .gitattributes from line-endings ├── .editorconfig from editorconfig ├── .gitignore ├── pyproject.toml the package and the manage- entry point ├── manager.yaml what is managed, from where, how it is verified ├── lib/ │ └── osat_manager_/ ├── tests/ │ ├── unit/ offline, run everywhere │ └── e2e/ │ └── linux/ one directory per platform run └── en-ca/ └── docs/ ├── README.md generated by uc-automa docs index ├── guides/ using the manager └── decisions/ decisions for this manager only ``` ## The process at a glance ```mermaid flowchart TD s1["Assess the tool on the radar"] s2["Record the decision"] s3["Create the repository"] s4["Subscribe to uc-automa"] s5["Describe the managed tool"] s6["Implement the manager"] s7["Test on each platform"] s8["Document"] s9["Release"] s10["Register and retire"] s1 --> s2 --> s3 --> s4 --> s5 --> s6 --> s7 --> s8 --> s9 --> s10 s7 -- "a platform fails" --> s6 ``` ## Assess the tool on the radar Every manager starts with the tool it manages, so the tool is evaluated before any code is written. Write a uc-radar entry using the radar's entry template and the Universal Cake evaluation metrics [(Steel, 2026d)](#ref-steel-2026d). Adding the entry to uc-radar goes through its own review; until then it is a draft. The entry answers the questions a manager depends on: - Does upstream publish prebuilt releases for Linux, macOS and Windows, and for which architectures? - Does upstream publish checksums, and are they signed? With what key? - Can the tool run from a user directory without installation or administrator rights? - What licence does the tool carry, and does it allow keeping a verified archive? - How often does upstream release, and how are versions named? Gate: the tool is in the `trial` or `adopt` ring, or the entry explains why a manager is still wanted. ## Record the decision Draft the decision to build the manager before the repository exists, outside any repository, such as in the hand-off folder for the work. It becomes `en-ca/docs/decisions/0001---v0.1.0.md`, numbered within the repository, in the repository's first commit. It names the managed tool, the radar entry, the platforms targeted first, and anything this manager does differently from the contract. Gate: the decision record is drafted. ## Create the repository Create the repository fresh and empty, with no forge-generated files, so its first commit already conforms. 1. Create the local repository with `git init`. Creating it on a forge and pushing are Christopher Steel's decisions, taken separately. 2. Generate the repository's identifier with `uuidgen -r`. 3. Write `.osat-manager-.assets/archive.yaml` and `dc.yaml`. 4. Place the drafted decision record at `en-ca/docs/decisions/0001---v0.1.0.md`, and commit it with the sidecar as the repository's first commit. ```yaml # .osat-manager-.assets/archive.yaml sat:role: "archive" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:" dc:title: "osat-manager-" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" ``` Gate: the first commit holds the sidecar and the decision record, and nothing else. ## Subscribe to uc-automa Everything shared arrives from uc-automa by subscription; nothing is copied by hand. Install uc-automa from its release tag into the environment you work in, together with uc-portage, which it depends on. uc-portage is not on a package index, so both are named in the same command; installing uc-automa alone fails to find it. ```sh python3 -m pip install "git+https://github.com/steelcj/uc-portage@v0.1.0" \ "git+https://github.com/steelcj/uc-automa@v0.1.0" uc-automa --version ``` The installed version is the one `init` pins, and every later `uc-automa` command requires the pin and the installed version to match (uc-automa 0020). `init` writes `.uc-automa.yaml` once, with the subscriptions the osat-manager layout requires (uc-automa 0023); the repository owns the file from then on. ```sh uc-automa init --repository osat-manager- --layout osat-manager uc-automa offerings plan uc-automa offerings apply git add -A git commit -m "Receive uc-automa offerings" ``` A repository that file-fairy served before, such as an existing manager moving to this process, still holds the blocks file-fairy managed, marked `` and ``, usually `claude-md-signpost` in `CLAUDE.md`. uc-portage takes over only blocks marked `` with a name its offerings deliver, and uc-automa delivers its signpost as `uc-automa-signpost`, so an old block is never taken over, and renaming its markers does not help. Delete each old `fairy:` block, markers and contents, by hand, in the same commit as the first apply; otherwise its stale text stays beside the new block. A licence that file-fairy delivered as a block now arrives as `LICENSE` and `LICENSES/` files instead. Gate: `uc-automa offerings plan` reports nothing to do, and no `fairy:begin` marker is left in the repository. ## Describe the managed tool Write `manager.yaml`, a declarative description of what the manager installs, where it comes from, how each download is verified, and what each platform needs. Keeping this in data rather than code means most managers differ only in this file, and a reviewer can check sources and verification without reading code. ```yaml # manager.yaml (illustrative; every value comes from the radar entry) tool: name: "" command: "manage-" upstream: "" license: "" versions: scheme: "semver" default_alias: "" versioned_alias: "-{major}.{minor}" sources: release_url: "" checksums_url: "" signature_url: "" verification: checksum: "sha256" signature: "" keep_verified_archive: true platforms: linux: {arch: ["x86_64", "aarch64"], status: "planned"} macos: {arch: ["x86_64", "arm64"], status: "planned"} windows: {arch: ["x86_64"], status: "planned"} ``` If upstream signs its checksums, pin its signing key by fingerprint, and confirm the fingerprint from two independent sources, such as upstream's documentation and the key server it names. Gate: every source and verification field is filled from the radar entry, with no placeholders left. ## Implement the manager Implement the contract in `lib/osat_manager_/`, reading `manager.yaml` for everything tool-specific, and expose it as a console-script entry point, which gives a native launcher on Windows and a script on Linux and macOS from one definition [(Python Packaging Authority, n.d.)](#ref-pypa-nd). - Standard library and `pathlib`, with no shell commands at runtime, so behaviour is the same on every platform. Tests may call other tools, such as `gpg`, to cross-check results. - Shared behaviour comes from the shared manager package (uc-automa 0024): reading `manager.yaml` without PyYAML, finding it in an install or a checkout, and verifying OpenPGP signatures. Until that package exists, a manager carries its own copies, listed as known debt. - A signature verifier is reviewed independently, by a reviewer who did not see it written, before any manager relying on it is tagged. - Platform differences, such as install locations and alias launchers, are resolved in one module. - Every download is verified with SHA-256 before it is unpacked, and against upstream's signature if upstream signs its checksums. The verified archive is kept. - `manager.yaml` is read from the repository root through the shared data resolver, so the installed package carries it (uc-automa 0019). Gate: `tests/unit/` passes offline. ## Test on each platform Each platform has its own end-to-end run, and each run updates the platform status table. A platform is either verified end to end or stated as not yet verified; it is never assumed (uc-automa 0011). | Platform | Where it runs | Record | | --- | --- | --- | | Linux | An Incus container restored to a clean snapshot before and after the run, as an ordinary user | `tests/e2e/linux/` | | Windows | The Windows 11 virtual machine, reached through its built-in OpenSSH Server with key authentication, as an ordinary user, restored to a snapshot before each run | `tests/e2e/windows/` | | macOS | Apple hardware, the only legitimate place to run macOS | `tests/e2e/macos/` | ```yaml # The end-to-end scenario every platform runs scenario: - "Install the manager into a clean user account" - "Install two versions of the managed tool side by side" - "Switch between them and confirm the active version" - "Rename an alias and confirm both forms resolve correctly" - "Attempt to modify an installed version and confirm it is protected" - "Remove a version, disconnect the network, and restore it from the verified archive" - "Uninstall the manager and confirm nothing is left behind" ``` A scenario run writes a record of every step beside its driver. Upstream files kept as test data, such as `SHA256SUMS`, keep their upstream names inside a zip file, because those names do not follow the naming directives. Gate: every platform in `manager.yaml` is `verified` or has a stated reason it is not. ## Document Write what a user needs, and nothing uc-automa already says. - `README.md`: what the manager manages, how to install it, and the platform status table from testing. - `en-ca/docs/guides/usage/using-manage--v0.1.0.md`: every command, with examples. - `ROADMAP.md`: what is planned, such as unverified platforms. - `CHANGELOG.md`: the entry for the first release, under `[Unreleased]`. - `uc-automa docs index`, to regenerate the documentation index. Gate: `uc-automa check` passes. ## Release The first release is 0.1.0. Until uc-automa provides the release ceremony, planned for uc-automa 0.2.0, a release is tagged by hand, and only with Christopher Steel's approval: a surgical commit that only rolls `CHANGELOG.md` to `## [0.1.0] - `, then an annotated tag `v0.1.0` whose message names the repository and the version, as the directive `release/annotated-version-tags` requires. A manager reaches 1.0.0 when every platform in `manager.yaml` is verified and the full scenario passes on each (uc-automa 0011); its documents then drop the version from their filenames (uc-automa 0002). Gate: the tag exists, approved. ## Register and retire Make the new manager findable, and retire what it replaces. 1. Update the tool's radar entry to link to the manager. 2. Add the manager to the list of OSAT managers, wherever that list is kept (see open questions). 3. If the manager replaces an older `osat-fluent--tool` repository, Christopher Steel adds a README notice naming the successor and archives the old repository, once the new repository is pushed, so the notice links to a real successor. It is not deleted or renamed, so every existing link and clone still works. Gate: a person starting from the radar entry, the OSAT list or the old repository arrives at the new manager. ## Checklist - [ ] Radar entry written for the tool, ring `trial` or `adopt` - [ ] Decision record drafted outside the repository - [ ] Repository created, first commit holding the sidecar and the decision record - [ ] uc-automa installed from its release tag, `uc-automa init` run, offerings applied and committed, old `fairy:` blocks removed - [ ] `manager.yaml` complete, with no placeholders - [ ] Manager implemented; unit tests pass offline - [ ] Linux, Windows and macOS each verified or stated as not yet verified - [ ] README, guide, roadmap and changelog written; `uc-automa check` passes - [ ] 0.1.0 tagged, with approval - [ ] Radar entry linked, manager listed, any predecessor archived with a notice ## Open questions - [ ] Where is the list of OSAT managers kept: in uc-automa, in uc-radar, or in its own repository? - [ ] Is `osat` the right directory name inside each platform's per-user data location? ## References Python Packaging Authority. (2026d). *uc-radar: Universal Cake radar entries and evaluation metrics* [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar [↩](#cite-steel-2026d) ## Changelog | Version | Date | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.4.0 | 2026-10-11 | Accepted | Subscribe stage: installing uc-automa and uc-portage from their release tags, and removing blocks file-fairy managed, which uc-portage never takes over | | 0.3.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Findings from building osat-manager-restic: the decision drafted before the repository and placed in its first commit, nothing left behind, the shared manager package, pinned keys confirmed twice, independent review of a verifier, snapshot-based Linux runs and the Windows route, upstream names inside zips, the release tag rule, archiving after push | | 0.2.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Revised to the foundation brief: uc-automa init and offerings instead of .automa.yaml and the interim file-fairy route, en-ca, the osat-manager layout, the three licences, by-hand tagging until the release ceremony, D11 settled; relicensed CC-BY-SA-4.0 | | 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | Draft | Initial process: manager contract, naming, layout, ten stages with gates, interim route, checklist | ## License This document, *Creating an OSAT Manager Repository*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

# UC Radar Entry Template

## Description

A raw markdown template used to create new uc-radar entries. The evaluation body follows the pillars defined in the current [Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics](#universal-cake-evaluation-metrics), so a completed entry and the metrics document use the same vocabulary throughout.

By default new entries go in the `assess` ring unless they document
an item that has been adopted informally and is currently relied upon
in dev, stage, or prod.

The radar uses five states, `assess`, `trial`, `adopt`, `hold`, and
`rejected`. See
[UC Radar Evaluation Lifecycle](#uc-radar--evaluation-lifecycle) for
the full state definitions and transitions.

## Notes

- The leading colon in the heading example below (`:hugo--static-site-generator`)
  is a legacy convention from an earlier naming version. Current slug
  convention per ADR-015 uses double hyphen as a grouping separator
  without a leading colon. This has not been reconciled with the

It recommends MinGit, taken directly from Git for Windows releases, as the manager's source, and the standard installer for client machines that a person will use directly. The git-scm.com download page does not list MinGit, so the recommendation rests on the release itself, whose checksums and signed tag make it verifiable. Three defaults in MinGit's system configuration need a deliberate decision before the manager ships. ## Sources and Acknowledgements The comparison applies *Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics* version 0.5.1 ([Steel, 2026](#apa-uc-metrics-reference)). The options come from the git-scm.com Windows download page ([Git Project, n.d.](#apa-gitscm-windows-reference)) and the Git for Windows 2.56.0.2 release behind it ([Git for Windows Project, 2026](#apa-gfw-release-reference)). Support periods come from the Git for Windows FAQ and its 32-bit support page. `MinGit-2.56.0.2-64-bit.zip` was downloaded, hashed, and unpacked on Linux to inspect its layout and configuration; no Windows binary was run. The evaluation was prepared with AI assistance from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic). ## Scope The subject is Git for Windows 2.56.0.2, released on 2026-10-05, in each of the forms it is offered. Git's own behaviour, and Git on Linux and macOS, are out of scope; for those platforms, dugite-native remains the candidate, pending its own entry. Network behaviour and accessibility of the Windows builds were not tested, since nothing was run on Windows. ## The options | Option | Artifact | What it is | Use | |---|---|---|---| | MinGit | `MinGit-2.56.0.2-64-bit.zip`, also ARM64 and 32-bit | Git for Windows' minimal build for applications that bundle Git: `git.exe` and its helpers, Git Credential Manager, no Bash, no GUI tools. 39.8 MB zip, 93 MB unpacked (verified) | osat-manager-git | | MinGit, busybox variant | `MinGit-2.56.0.2-busybox-64-bit.zip`, also ARM64 and 32-bit | MinGit with BusyBox in place of the standard Unix tools; smaller, less compatible | None | | PortableGit | `PortableGit-2.56.0.2-64-bit.7z.exe`, also ARM64 | Full Git for Windows, including Git Bash, unpacked into any folder with no registry or PATH changes; a self-extracting 7-Zip archive that 7-Zip can open without running it | Optional full variant for the manager | | Full archive | `Git-2.56.0.2-64-bit.tar.bz2`, also ARM64 | The full Git as a plain archive | Alternative to PortableGit | | Standalone installer | `Git-2.56.0.2-64-bit.exe`, also ARM64 | Full Git for Windows with Git Bash, Git GUI, gitk, Explorer menus, and PATH changes | Client machines, git-cola | | winget | `winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget` | The standalone installer, through Microsoft's package manager | Client setup where winget is present | | Build from source | Git for Windows repository | Compile it yourself | None | The git-scm.com page lists only the installer, PortableGit, winget, and source. MinGit, its busybox variants, and the full archives appear only on the release. ## The decisive observation The osat-manager pattern needs an artifact it can download, verify against a published checksum, unpack into a versioned directory, and point an alias at, with no installer and no system changes. MinGit is exactly that, and it is published by Git for Windows itself for this purpose. The installer and winget fail the pattern by design, since they decide where things go. PortableGit fits, but carries Git Bash and much more than a manager needs, so it suits an optional "full" variant rather than the default. dugite-native, the other candidate surveyed earlier, builds its Windows packages by repackaging MinGit. Taking MinGit at its source removes GitHub Desktop's packaging from the Windows dependency chain without losing anything. ## Gates for Git for Windows | Gate | Result | Evidence | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Telemetry or content exposure that cannot be disabled | Pass | Inferred | Git has no telemetry. Git Credential Manager contacts a hosting service only when credentials are requested for it. Not traced on Windows | | A licence incompatible with the project | Pass, for use | Verified | Git is GPL-2.0-only; the bundled `LICENSE.txt` states that only version 2 applies. Using MinGit raises no issue, and redistributing it carries the GPL's usual source obligations; Git's code cannot be combined into AGPL-3.0-or-later or GPL-3.0-or-later works | | Failure of the accessibility floor | Pass | Inferred | MinGit is a command-line tool with no interface of its own. The installer's accessibility was not tested | | No exit | Pass | Verified | Repositories are plain Git. Removing MinGit means deleting its directory | ## Verification The release notes carry a SHA-256 table covering every asset, the release tag is GPG-signed by the Git for Windows maintainer, and the executables carry Authenticode signatures (claimed by the release page). The downloaded MinGit zip hashed to `da35e72aa21c005a5a0d298cfbae110bc1609a815730ea0dde84b01a1b3cd3be`, matching the release notes (verified). The git-scm.com page itself publishes no checksums. The table is markdown inside the release notes, not a SHA256SUMS file, so the manager must parse it, unlike osat-manager-python, which reads python-build-standalone's SHA256SUMS. GitHub's release API may report a per-asset digest, which would be simpler; that could not be checked here and should be confirmed when the manager is built. ## Older systems Git for Windows supports Windows 8.1 and later, on x64 and ARM64 ([Git for Windows Project, n.d.-a](#apa-gfw-faq-reference)). Older systems can only run frozen releases. | System | Last Git for Windows release | |---|---| | Windows 7 and 8 | 2.46.2 | | Windows Vista and Server 2008 | 2.37.1 | | 32-bit, installer and PortableGit | 2.48.1 | | 32-bit, MinGit only | Supported until April 2029 | The 32-bit dates come from the project's support page ([Git for Windows Project, n.d.-b](#apa-gfw-32bit-reference)). A manager could pin 2.46.2 for a Windows 7 client, as the psutil entry suggests pinning 7.2.x for older Python, but that machine gets no further Git security fixes. Client-facing guidance should say so plainly. ## Recommendation | Option | Ring | For | |---|---|---| | MinGit, from Git for Windows releases | Trial | osat-manager-git's Windows source | | PortableGit | Assess | An optional full variant of the manager, for users who want Git Bash | | Standalone installer, or winget | Assess | Client machines a person uses directly, and git-cola, whose README asks for it | | MinGit busybox variants | Hold | Less compatible, no offsetting benefit | | Building from source | Hold | The official builds already meet the need | | Frozen releases for Windows 7, 8, or Vista | Hold | Only as a declared bridge, with the security cost stated | MinGit moves to Adopt when osat-manager-git installs, switches, and removes it end to end on real Windows hardware, with these decisions made and recorded in its proposal: - **Line endings.** MinGit's system configuration sets `core.autocrlf = true`. The manager should either install Git LFS beside MinGit or tell the user plainly. - **Inherited configuration.** MinGit's system configuration includes `C:/Program Files/Git/etc/gitconfig` and its 32-bit counterpart, so on a machine that also has a full Git for Windows install, MinGit inherits that install's settings. The manager should document this or override it. - **Paths.** The 2.56 layout places Git's runtime under `ucrt64`, after a migration from `mingw64`. Aliases should target `cmd\git.exe`, the stable entry point, rather than paths inside the runtime directory. ## Flip conditions - If Git for Windows stops publishing 64-bit MinGit, the manager falls back to the full `tar.bz2` archive, which needs no installer either. - If users mostly want Git Bash, PortableGit becomes the default and MinGit the minimal option. - If checksum parsing from release notes proves fragile, and no API digest is available, verify against the signed tag by building, or pin by hash per version as osat-manager-python's archive already allows. ## Relationship to project This entry gives osat-manager-git its Windows half. On Linux and macOS the candidate remains dugite-native, whose builds need relocation variables in the alias wrapper, link the system's libcurl for HTTPS, and require glibc 2.34; that candidate needs its own entry. git-cola, evaluated separately, needs Git on the path and would be a natural consumer of the manager. ## Status notes - Last reviewed: 2026-10-11 - In assess: the automated pass recommends MinGit for Trial as the manager's Windows source. It records the gate results, a scorecard, the findings that shaped the ratings, and a recommendation for the radar. mingit passes all four default gates for personal use: it makes no network contact, holds no data, and is trivially replaced. Its problems are in how it gets onto and off a machine, and in its own correctness. The npm installer edits shell start-up files in ways that can damage them, the documented uninstall path does not work with current npm, arguments containing spaces are split apart, and one documented command fails. The licence situation is also untidy. We recommend leaving it in Assess and meeting the same need with git's own alias mechanism. ## Sources and Acknowledgements The evaluation applies *Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics* version 0.5.1 ([Steel, 2026](#apa-uc-metrics-reference)). Facts about mingit come from files in the mingit repository, read directly at commit `f893664a` on 2026-10-11, from the 2.4.0 package published on npm, from the npm registry's metadata for mingit and its dependencies, and from installing, using, and uninstalling that package under a test home directory with every relevant system call traced. The evaluation was prepared with AI assistance from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic). ## Scope We evaluate mingit 2.4.0, the current release on npm, as a personal developer tool for interactive shells. All 32 connections in the run came from npm's own processes, to the npm registry's address range and DNS; none came from mingit's `install.js`, `postinstall.js`, or the shell script they start. Tracing those scripts on their own confirmed it: no network calls, and exactly two writes, creating `~/.mingit.sh` and appending to `~/.bashrc`. At runtime, mingit is a shell function named `g` that maps an abbreviation to a git subcommand and passes anything else straight to `git` ([mingit Project, n.d.-c](#apa-mingit-bashrc-reference)). It has no network or storage code of its own. ### Changes to shell start-up files On Linux, the installer copies the function to `~/.mingit.sh` and appends `source ~/.mingit.sh` to `~/.bashrc` with `echo ... >>` ([mingit Project, n.d.-d](#apa-mingit-installsh-reference)). That has three consequences we reproduced. First, the append does not begin with a newline. Our test `~/.bashrc` ended with `export FOO=1` and no trailing newline, as files saved by some editors do. After install the line read `export FOO=1source ~/.mingit.sh`; a new shell set `FOO` to `1source`, printed an error, and did not load mingit. The user's own setting was silently changed. Second, the install does not check for an existing entry, so reinstalling or upgrading adds a second `source` line each time. Third, removal does not work as documented. After a reinstall, the remaining line made every new bash session print a "No such file or directory" error. On Windows the installer appends with no newline at all, and on macOS with zsh it appends a block that also runs `compinit -u` ([mingit Project, n.d.-b](#apa-mingit-install-reference)). These were read from source, not run. ### Correctness of the function Every case in the `g` function except `c` passes arguments as unquoted `$@`, so bash splits any argument containing a space and expands any glob. The Windows variant lacks the completion mapping for `g f`. ### Licence The only licence statement is `"license": "ISC"` in `package.json` ([mingit Project, n.d.-f](#apa-mingit-package-reference)). It recommends MinGit, taken directly from Git for Windows releases, as the manager's source, and the standard installer for client machines that a person will use directly. The git-scm.com download page does not list MinGit, so the recommendation rests on the release itself, whose checksums and signed tag make it verifiable. Three defaults in MinGit's system configuration need a deliberate decision before the manager ships. 65 66 ## Sources and Acknowledgements 67 68 The comparison applies *Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics* version 0.5.1 ([Steel, 2026](#apa-uc-metrics-reference)). The options come from the git-scm.com Windows download page ([Git Project, n.d.](#apa-gitscm-windows-reference)) and the Git for Windows 2.56.0.2 release behind it ([Git for Windows Project, 2026](#apa-gfw-release-reference)). Support periods come from the Git for Windows FAQ and its 32-bit support page. `MinGit-2.56.0.2-64-bit.zip` was downloaded, hashed, and unpacked on Linux to inspect its layout and configuration; no Windows binary was run. The evaluation was prepared with AI assistance from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic). 69 70 ## Scope 71 72 The subject is Git for Windows 2.56.0.2, released on 2026-10-05, in each of the forms it is offered. Git's own behaviour, and Git on Linux and macOS, are out of scope; for those platforms, dugite-native remains the candidate, pending its own entry. Network behaviour and accessibility of the Windows builds were not tested, since nothing was run on Windows. 73 74 ## The options 75 76 | Option | Artifact | What it is | Use | 77 |---|---|---|---| 78 | MinGit | `MinGit-2.56.0.2-64-bit.zip`, also ARM64 and 32-bit | Git for Windows' minimal build for applications that bundle Git: `git.exe` and its helpers, Git Credential Manager, no Bash, no GUI tools. 39.8 MB zip, 93 MB unpacked (verified) | osat-manager-git | 79 | MinGit, busybox variant | `MinGit-2.56.0.2-busybox-64-bit.zip`, also ARM64 and 32-bit | MinGit with BusyBox in place of the standard Unix tools; smaller, less compatible | None | 80 | PortableGit | `PortableGit-2.56.0.2-64-bit.7z.exe`, also ARM64 | Full Git for Windows, including Git Bash, unpacked into any folder with no registry or PATH changes; a self-extracting 7-Zip archive that 7-Zip can open without running it | Optional full variant for the manager | 81 | Full archive | `Git-2.56.0.2-64-bit.tar.bz2`, also ARM64 | The full Git as a plain archive | Alternative to PortableGit | 82 | Standalone installer | `Git-2.56.0.2-64-bit.exe`, also ARM64 | Full Git for Windows with Git Bash, Git GUI, gitk, Explorer menus, and PATH changes | Client machines, git-cola | 83 | winget | `winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget` | The standalone installer, through Microsoft's package manager | Client setup where winget is present | 84 | Build from source | Git for Windows repository | Compile it yourself | None | 85 86 The git-scm.com page lists only the installer, PortableGit, winget, and source. MinGit, its busybox variants, and the full archives appear only on the release. 87 88 ## The decisive observation 89 90 The osat-manager pattern needs an artifact it can download, verify against a published checksum, unpack into a versioned directory, and point an alias at, with no installer and no system changes. MinGit is exactly that, and it is published by Git for Windows itself for this purpose. The installer and winget fail the pattern by design, since they decide where things go. PortableGit fits, but carries Git Bash and much more than a manager needs, so it suits an optional "full" variant rather than the default. 91 92 dugite-native, the other candidate surveyed earlier, builds its Windows packages by repackaging MinGit. Taking MinGit at its source removes GitHub Desktop's packaging from the Windows dependency chain without losing anything. 93 94 ## Gates for Git for Windows 95 96 | Gate | Result | Evidence | Notes | 97 |---|---|---|---| 98 | Telemetry or content exposure that cannot be disabled | Pass | Inferred | Git has no telemetry. Git Credential Manager contacts a hosting service only when credentials are requested for it. Not traced on Windows | 99 | A licence incompatible with the project | Pass, for use | Verified | Git is GPL-2.0-only; the bundled `LICENSE.txt` states that only version 2 applies. Using MinGit raises no issue, and redistributing it carries the GPL's usual source obligations; Git's code cannot be combined into AGPL-3.0-or-later or GPL-3.0-or-later works | 100 | Failure of the accessibility floor | Pass | Inferred | MinGit is a command-line tool with no interface of its own. The installer's accessibility was not tested | 101 | No exit | Pass | Verified | Repositories are plain Git. Removing MinGit means deleting its directory | 102 103 ## Verification 104 105 The release notes carry a SHA-256 table covering every asset, the release tag is GPG-signed by the Git for Windows maintainer, and the executables carry Authenticode signatures (claimed by the release page). The downloaded MinGit zip hashed to `da35e72aa21c005a5a0d298cfbae110bc1609a815730ea0dde84b01a1b3cd3be`, matching the release notes (verified). The git-scm.com page itself publishes no checksums. 106 107 The table is markdown inside the release notes, not a SHA256SUMS file, so the manager must parse it, unlike osat-manager-python, which reads python-build-standalone's SHA256SUMS. GitHub's release API may report a per-asset digest, which would be simpler; that could not be checked here and should be confirmed when the manager is built. 108 109 ## Older systems 110 111 Git for Windows supports Windows 8.1 and later, on x64 and ARM64 ([Git for Windows Project, n.d.-a](#apa-gfw-faq-reference)). Older systems can only run frozen releases. 112 113 | System | Last Git for Windows release | 114 |---|---| 115 | Windows 7 and 8 | 2.46.2 | 116 | Windows Vista and Server 2008 | 2.37.1 | 117 | 32-bit, installer and PortableGit | 2.48.1 | 118 | 32-bit, MinGit only | Supported until April 2029 | 119 120 The 32-bit dates come from the project's support page ([Git for Windows Project, n.d.-b](#apa-gfw-32bit-reference)). A manager could pin 2.46.2 for a Windows 7 client, as the psutil entry suggests pinning 7.2.x for older Python, but that machine gets no further Git security fixes. Client-facing guidance should say so plainly. 121 122 ## Recommendation 123 124 | Option | Ring | For | 125 |---|---|---| 126 | MinGit, from Git for Windows releases | Trial | osat-manager-git's Windows source | 127 | PortableGit | Assess | An optional full variant of the manager, for users who want Git Bash | 128 | Standalone installer, or winget | Assess | Client machines a person uses directly, and git-cola, whose README asks for it | 129 | MinGit busybox variants | Hold | Less compatible, no offsetting benefit | 130 | Building from source | Hold | The official builds already meet the need | 131 | Frozen releases for Windows 7, 8, or Vista | Hold | Only as a declared bridge, with the security cost stated | 132 133 MinGit moves to Adopt when osat-manager-git installs, switches, and removes it end to end on real Windows hardware, with these decisions made and recorded in its proposal: 134 135 - **Line endings.** MinGit's system configuration sets `core.autocrlf = true`. For SAT content repositories shared between Linux and Windows, decide whether the manager keeps this default or sets `autocrlf` per repository, preferably with a `.gitattributes` policy in the repositories themselves. 136 - **Git LFS.** The same configuration declares the `lfs` filter with `required = true`, but MinGit ships no `git-lfs` executable (verified). A checkout of any repository that uses LFS will fail. The manager should either install Git LFS beside MinGit or tell the user plainly. 137 - **Inherited configuration.** MinGit's system configuration includes `C:/Program Files/Git/etc/gitconfig` and its 32-bit counterpart, so on a machine that also has a full Git for Windows install, MinGit inherits that install's settings. The manager should document this or override it. 138 - **Paths.** The 2.56 layout places Git's runtime under `ucrt64`, after a migration from `mingw64`. Aliases should target `cmd\git.exe`, the stable entry point, rather than paths inside the runtime directory. 139 140 ## Flip conditions 141 142 - If Git for Windows stops publishing 64-bit MinGit, the manager falls back to the full `tar.bz2` archive, which needs no installer either. 143 - If users mostly want Git Bash, PortableGit becomes the default and MinGit the minimal option. 144 - If checksum parsing from release notes proves fragile, and no API digest is available, verify against the signed tag by building, or pin by hash per version as osat-manager-python's archive already allows. 145 146 ## Relationship to project 147 148 This entry gives osat-manager-git its Windows half. On Linux and macOS the candidate remains dugite-native, whose builds need relocation variables in the alias wrapper, link the system's libcurl for HTTPS, and require glibc 2.34; that candidate needs its own entry. git-cola, evaluated separately, needs Git on the path and would be a natural consumer of the manager. 149 150 ## Status notes 151 152 - Last reviewed: 2026-10-11 153 - In assess: the automated pass recommends MinGit for Trial as the manager's Windows source. What moves it to Adopt is the manager working end to end on real Windows, with the four decisions above recorded in its proposal. 154 - Re-review triggers: a change in how Git for Windows publishes checksums, any change to MinGit's default system configuration, and the end of 32-bit MinGit in April 2029. 155 156 ## License 157 158 This document, *Git on Windows, Options for osat-manager-git*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html). 159 160 ## Resources 161 162 ### Evaluation framework 163 164 - [Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics](#apa-uc-metrics-reference) 165 166 ### Git for Windows 167 168 - [Install Git on Windows, git-scm.com](#apa-gitscm-windows-reference) 169 - [Release 2.56.0.windows.2](#apa-gfw-release-reference) 170 - [FAQ, supported Windows versions](#apa-gfw-faq-reference) 171 - [32-bit support](#apa-gfw-32bit-reference) 172 173 ## References 174 175 Git for Windows Project.
