Its conda backend already does what manage-git would do on Linux and macOS, so it's the model to copy, not something to depend on. Main risks: only one person can change its core, and some tools still install through asdf plugins.
- **Entire** (`assess/ai-collaboration/universal-cake-evaluation--entire--agent-session-capture-and-git-hosting-v0-1-0.md`): it covers every product listed on entire.io.
  - **The CLI (MIT):** worth a private trial for tracking which AI work produced which code.
  - **Its defaults are the problem:** it pushes full session transcripts with every `git push`, and sends usage analytics to PostHog unless you turn it off.
  - **The hosted services:** I put them on Hold for client data. Entire is a Delaware company that can change its terms at any time, has no Canadian region and publishes no pricing.

# Vishpala — Eleventy + Sveltia CMS MVP

Static site built by [Eleventy](https://www.11ty.dev/), authored through [Sveltia CMS](https://github.com/sveltia/sveltia-cms), with internationalization modeled through Dublin Core `identifier`/`relation` front matter rather than a locale-pairing feature baked into the CMS or the framework.

## Run it

```sh
npm install
npm run build  # writes ./_site
npm start      # dev server with rebuild-on-save, http://localhost:8080
```

## The content model

```
content/
├── en-ca/
│   ├── en-ca.json          ← directory data: locale, language, layout
│   ├── index.md
│   └── about/
│       ├── index.md
│       ├── index.assets/hero.svg
│       └── legal/
│           ├── privacy.md
│           └── privacy.assets/diagram.svg
└── fr-ca/                  ← same shape, mirrored (not identical) content
```

Two conventions, both read straight off the filesystem — nothing is hand-registered:

- **A folder's own page is `index.md`.** `about/index.md` is the page for `/about/`. Its sibling `index.assets/` folder holds its images, matched by the `index` filename stem.
- **A leaf page that has no children of its own is `name.md` directly inside its parent folder**, e.g. `legal/privacy.md`. Its assets live in `privacy.assets/`, next to it, matched by the `privacy` stem. `legal/` itself has no `index.md` — it's a pure grouping folder, and still shows up in the nav as an unlinked section label so `privacy` stays reachable.

Every `.md` file carries two Dublin Core fields:

```yaml
title: "About"
identifier: "urn:uuid:8a1e2f3b-…"   # unique to THIS file (this Expression)
relation: "urn:uuid:ffdca22b-…"     # shared Work UUID — same on every
                                    # locale's version of this page
```

### Manual generation of a random UUID's using UUID version 4

Version 4 UUIDs are generated from random or pseudo-random data.

```bash
uuidgen -r
```

### identifier

The `identifier` names the unique ***Expression*** of a ***Work***. In the case the ***Work*** is the idea or concept of an About page, expressed in English using the content in this particular markdown document.

#### Why we do it this way

#### Allows for multilingual filenames and more 

This opens up a very powerful mechanism. It enables the creation of relationships between unique ***Expression*** of a ***Work***.

So an About page filename and it's entire path or URL can all be translated into other ***Expressions*** in any human language available for systems, like, English, Spanish and French.

#### Accessible content as alternative Expressions

Leveraging this same method also allows for alternative **Expressions** of the same **Work** in every language.

In other words, a relationship 

It also enables alternative expressions of the same idea, in this case, an about page, that can be created  So this allows us to have multiple about pages in multiple languages

#### relation

 `relation` names the original Work it realizes.

Two files in different locale folders that share the same `relation` are treated as translations of one another; that's the entire mechanism the language switcher runs on.

Nothing about locale pairing lives in filenames, folder names, or CMS config — it's just a shared UUID in front matter, so it holds up if you later add more Expressions of the same Work (a grade-7 rewrite, an AAC rendering) without redesigning the pairing mechanism.

## What the build derives from the filesystem

`.eleventy.js` + `_11ty/nav-tree.js`:

- **`collections.navTrees[locale]`** — a nested tree built from every page's URL, one per locale, used by `_includes/partials/nav.njk` to render the sidebar menu. Add a folder, get a nav entry; no manual menu file to maintain. Sibling ordering is `order` (front matter, default last) then alphabetical by title.
- **`collections.byWork`** — every page grouped by its `relation` UUID, used by `_includes/partials/language-switcher.njk` to link a page to its sibling Expressions in other locales.
- **One deliberate permalink override** (`content/content.11tydata.js`):
  Eleventy's default "pretty URL" behavior would turn `privacy.md` into `privacy/index.html`, a directory deeper than `privacy.assets/`, which breaks the relative image path written in the source. Leaf (non-index) pages are instead output flat as `privacy.html`, staying in the same directory as their own assets folder. `index.md` pages already avoid this problem by default and are left alone.

## Sveltia CMS (`admin/config.yml`)

**Superseded — see "CMS structure: File Collections" further down for the current, accurate description.** Originally a folder collection per locale; migrated to File Collections after confirming Sveltia can't create nested folders through its UI. One thing worth noting explicitly since it was flagged as a real gap at the time: the old design couldn't *author* the `legal/privacy.md`-style flat leaf pattern through the CMS at all — File Collections' literal per-page paths close that gap for free, since `privacy` is just another explicit `files:` entry now, no special-casing needed.

The `media_folder`/`public_folder` relative-path setup for per-entry `index.assets/` folders is written the way current Decap-compatible docs describe it, but that resolution behavior has changed across CMS versions before, worth a smoke test against a real Sveltia CMS instance rather than trusting it blind.

`backend.name: git-gateway` is also still a placeholder. Point it at  github`/`gitlab`/whatever actually hosts this repo, and set `repo`, before this goes near production.

## SEO: canonical + hreflang (`_includes/partials/i18n-meta.njk`)

Every page emits a self-referencing `<link rel="canonical">` and, when it has a `relation`, one `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="…">` per sibling Expression plus one `hreflang="x-default"` pointing at the Work's default locale (`_11ty/site-config.js`, currently `en-ca`). All of it comes from `collections.byWork`, the same collection the visible language switcher reads, so the machine-readable linkage can't drift from what's shown in the UI.

 `site.url` is currently set to `https://vishpala.com` in `site-config.js`, confirm that's the real production origin before this goes live.

## Missing-translation handling (`partials/language-switcher.njk`)

The switcher now enumerates every locale that exists anywhere on the site (`collections.locales`), not just the ones with an Expression of the current Work. A locale with no Expression renders as a visibly muted link to that locale's home page, with a title/aria note explaining it's not translated yet, instead of just quietly not appearing.

Front matter `localeExclusive: true` opts a page out of that treatment entirely (for content that will never have a translation, vs. content that's simply pending one). See `content/en-ca/careers/index.md` (pending, shows the fallback + build warning) vs. `content/en-ca/press/index.md`'s where (`localeExclusive`, shows neither).

## Build-time validation (`_11ty/validate.js`)

Runs on every build via the `i18nValidation` collection. Catches:

- malformed `identifier`/`relation` values (must match `urn:uuid:…`)
- an `identifier` reused across more than one file
- a `relation` with more than one Expression in the *same* locale (probably not what you meant)
- a `relation` that only exists in one locale and isn't marked `localeExclusive` — usually means a translation is pending, or a typo broke the pairing on the other locale's page

All of the above print as `[i18n] warning:` / `[i18n] error:` to the console. Errors don't fail the build by default (so a typo doesn't block someone from previewing their edit) — set `ELEVENTY_STRICT=1` to make errors throw, e.g. in CI: `ELEVENTY_STRICT=1 npm run build`.

## CMS structure: File Collections, not Folder Collections (`admin/config.yml`)

These aren't a compliance checklist. They're the practical form of
Universal Cake — our own framework for asking, before building or
choosing anything, who it actually serves and what it costs the people
who depend on it if that relationship goes wrong. Universal Cake starts
from the most fundamental requirements and builds up: a site nobody can
read can't deliver on anything else it promises.

## Accessibility

Our first commitment, because it's the one everything else depends on.
A site that's unreadable to someone using a screen reader, unusable on
an old device, or written in a language a visitor doesn't speak, has
failed before anything else about it matters. That includes people with
vision, hearing, motor, and speech differences, and it includes economic
and cognitive accessibility — whether something is affordable, learnable
without training, and forgiving of mistakes.

## Sustainability

We try not to spend other people's bandwidth, battery, or electricity by
default. Concretely, not aspirationally: every font this site uses is
served from our own servers, not fetched from a third party's — no
request to Google Fonts or any other external service just to render
text. It's a small thing on its own, and it's the kind of small thing
that adds up across millions of page loads, and across visitors on
slower or less reliable connections than the one this was built on.

## Sovereignty

You shouldn't have to trust our word that you could leave if you needed
to — you should be able to check. Every page of this site is a plain
text file, in an open format, tracked in version control. If the tools
we build with disappeared tomorrow, the content wouldn't disappear with
them.

## Data Portability

Closely tied to sovereignty, and worth naming on its own: nothing here
is locked behind a proprietary export process. What's readable by a
program is also readable by a person — a technically complete export
that only a developer can open isn't the same guarantee as one anyone
can.

## Longevity

We can't promise any particular tool we use today will still exist in
ten years — nobody honestly can. What we can commit to is choosing
plain, open formats and widely-used, forkable tools over proprietary or
fashionable ones, specifically so that the content outlives whatever
we're currently using to build it.

We are a studio of practitioners in technology, design, and
infrastructure — working with individuals and organisations who want
to operate with greater agency.

## Who we are

Vishpala is a multidisciplinary studio. We are technologists,
designers, and infrastructure specialists who work together on
problems that require all three disciplines to solve well.

We take our name from the Rigvedic figure Vishpala — a warrior who
loses a leg in battle and is given an iron prosthetic by the Ashvins
so she can return to the field. We are interested in the idea of
prosthetics: tools and infrastructure that extend capability, restore
agency, and allow people to do what they came to do.

## What we believe

**Sovereignty matters.** Organisations that depend entirely on
infrastructure they do not control are fragile in ways that are not
always visible until something breaks. We help organisations
understand their dependencies and, where it serves them, reduce them.

**Accessibility is not optional.** We do not build things that exclude
people with disabilities, and we do not help other organisations build
them. WCAG 2.2 Level AA is the floor we hold our own client work to.

**Complexity should be proportionate.** The right infrastructure for a
community organisation is not the right infrastructure for a national
one. We size solutions to the actual operational capacity of the
people who will maintain them.

**Excellence takes time.** We work on fewer things at once than most
studios. We do not take on work we cannot do well.

## How we work

We work in close collaboration with our clients throughout a project —
not in isolation with periodic check-ins. We believe the people who
will use and maintain what we build should understand it, which means
building understanding as we go rather than handing over a finished
system at the end.

We work in English and French.

Our commitment to accessibility, and the current state of this site.

## Commitment

Accessibility is the first of our [commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/),
because everything else this site does depends on it. We treat it as a
core discipline of our practice, not a compliance exercise bolted on
at the end.

## Current measures

This site has been designed and built with accessibility as a primary
requirement. The following measures are in place:

- Semantic HTML structure with appropriate landmark regions
- A "Skip to content" link as the first focusable element on every page
- Every interactive part of the site — the language switcher, the mobile menu, all navigation links — works from a keyboard alone, with visible focus outlines on every focusable element
- The mobile menu is a native `<details>`/`<summary>` disclosure rather than a custom JavaScript widget, so it behaves the way assistive technology already expects
- Nothing on this site depends on JavaScript to be readable or navigable
- Every page declares its own language (`lang="en"` or `lang="fr"`) and alternate-language links (`hreflang`)
- Where a page has no translation yet, the language switcher shows it as missing rather than linking somewhere broken
- Meaningful images carry descriptive alt text; decorative ones don't compete for a screen reader's attention
- Diagrams are plain SVG, not flattened screenshots, so their content stays selectable and scalable
- Text resizes fluidly with the browser's own zoom and font-size settings, rather than being fixed to a pixel size
- Fonts are self-hosted (see [Commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/)), so text still renders even when a third-party font host would otherwise block or slow the page
- Layout reflows for narrow screens and enlarged text without content being clipped or overlapping

## Known limitations

This statement describes intent and current practice, not a certified
audit or a claimed conformance level. If something on this site
doesn't work the way it's described here, that's a bug we want to
know about.

No known issues at time of publication.

## Feedback and contact

If you encounter an accessibility barrier on this site — something
that prevents you from accessing content or using a feature — tell us
what page you were on and what happened:

Email: accessibility@vishpala.com

We treat accessibility reports as a priority fix, not a backlog item.

Our commitment to privacy as a foundational principle — not a
compliance exercise. For the minimal, factual account of what this
particular site collects, see the [Privacy Policy](/en-ca/about/legal/privacy/);
this page is about the principle behind it.

## Principle

Privacy at Vishpala is not a legal obligation we satisfy at minimum
cost. It is a foundational design principle that shapes every decision
about what we build, what data we collect, and what infrastructure we
use.

We apply the seven foundational principles of Privacy by Design as
articulated by Ann Cavoukian:

- Proactive, not reactive — preventive, not remedial
- Privacy as the default setting
- Privacy embedded into design
- Full functionality — positive-sum, not zero-sum
- End-to-end security — full lifecycle protection
- Visibility and transparency
- Respect for user privacy — keep it user-centric

## What we collect and why

**This website** — we do not use analytics tracking. We do not set
cookies. We do not load third-party scripts. No data about visitors to
this site is collected, transmitted to third parties, or retained.

**Client engagements** — we collect the information necessary to
deliver our work: contact information, project materials, and
communications. We do not collect information beyond what is needed.
We do not retain client data beyond the period required for the
engagement and any applicable legal retention requirement.

**Communications** — email and other communications with us are
stored on infrastructure we operate. We do not use email marketing
platforms or CRM systems that transmit your contact information to
third parties.

## Your rights

Under the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
(PIPEDA) and applicable provincial privacy legislation, you have the
right to:

- Know what personal information we hold about you
- Access that information
- Request correction of inaccurate information
- Withdraw consent for processing where consent is the legal basis
- Have your information deleted, subject to legal retention requirements

To exercise any of these rights, contact us at privacy@vishpala.com.

## Infrastructure

Our fonts are self-hosted — no request to Google Fonts or any other
third party just to render text. See [Commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/)
for the rest of what that principle covers on this site.

## Contact

Questions about this policy or about how we handle personal
information: privacy@vishpala.com.

Our commitment to environmental and operational sustainability in the
work we do and how we do it.

## Principle

We build things that are meant to last. That commitment extends beyond
the technical quality of the work to its environmental and operational
footprint.

Sustainability at Vishpala means building systems that consume the
minimum necessary resources, that can be maintained by small teams
without specialised infrastructure, and that do not accumulate
complexity faster than the capacity to understand and operate them.

## Digital sustainability

**Efficient infrastructure** — we design systems sized to actual
workload. We do not recommend infrastructure at a scale that requires
constant management overhead to justify its cost or complexity.
Smaller, simpler, better-understood systems are almost always more
sustainable than large, complex ones.

**Minimal dependencies** — every dependency is a liability: a thing
that must be updated, monitored, and eventually replaced. We minimise
dependencies as a matter of practice, preferring solutions that
compose well from smaller, stable components over solutions that
introduce large dependency trees.

**Long-lived software** — we prefer technologies with long track
records and stable interfaces over technologies that require frequent
rewrites to remain current. The most sustainable software is software
that does not need to be replaced.

**No unnecessary data collection** — collecting data has an energy
cost. Storing data has an energy cost. Transmitting data has an energy
cost. We do not collect, store, or transmit data that does not serve a
clear purpose.

## Operational sustainability

**Documentation** — undocumented systems are unsustainable systems.
They accumulate technical debt invisibly and become dependent on the
continued availability of the people who built them. We treat
documentation as a core deliverable.

**Knowledge transfer** — we build with the intention that our clients
can operate, maintain, and extend what we build without us. Dependency
on an external consultant is not a sustainable operational model.

**Workload** — we do not take on more work than we can do well.
Overextended practitioners produce lower quality work and burn out. We
maintain a sustainable pace as a matter of professional principle.

## What we do not yet do

We do not currently measure or report the specific energy consumption
of the infrastructure we operate or recommend. This is a gap we intend
to address. We will update this commitment when we have a methodology
we are confident in.

Conformance, remediation, and the organisational practice of building
things that work for everyone.

Accessibility is not a checklist or a compliance exercise. It is the
practice of building things that work for the full range of people who
need to use them — across abilities, devices, languages, and connection
speeds.

We approach accessibility as a discipline that runs through every stage
of a project, not a phase that happens after design and development are
complete. The cost of retrofitting accessibility is always higher than
building it in from the start.

## What we work on

**Conformance audits** — systematic evaluation of digital products
against WCAG 2.2 criteria, delivered as a prioritised remediation plan
with clear ownership and testable acceptance criteria. We audit to AA
as standard and AAA where the use case warrants it.

**Remediation** — hands-on remediation of accessibility issues in
HTML, CSS, and content, including complex cases involving dynamic
content, single-page applications, and custom interactive components.

**Procurement support** — accessibility requirements for RFPs and
vendor evaluation criteria, including evaluation of VPAT documentation
and independent testing of vendor claims.

**Organisational practice** — training, process integration, and
tooling recommendations that build accessibility competence into a
team's standard workflow rather than concentrating it in a single
specialist.

**Usability testing** — moderated testing sessions with participants
who use assistive technologies, screen readers, switch access, voice
control, and other access methods, delivering qualitative findings
that automated tools cannot surface.

## Our approach

Automated testing catches approximately 30% of accessibility issues.
The rest require human judgment. We combine automated scanning with
manual expert review and user testing because no single method is
sufficient on its own.

Accessible, multilingual design systems built to serve people — not to
impress peers or satisfy platform requirements.

We practice design as a discipline of clarity. Our work begins with the
people who will use it — their actual contexts, access levels,
languages, and needs — and builds outward from there toward visual
form, not the other way around.

Design at Vishpala is inseparable from accessibility. We treat WCAG 2.2
Level AA conformance as a floor, not a ceiling, and we test with real
people across a range of abilities and assistive technologies at every
stage of a project.

## What we work on

**Design systems** — token-based, component-level design
infrastructure that can be maintained by a small team, translated
without visual degradation, and extended without breaking existing
patterns. We build for longevity, not for the current sprint.

**Accessible interfaces** — visual design, interaction design, and
content design that work for people with a wide range of visual,
motor, cognitive, and linguistic access needs. We conduct usability
testing as a standard part of every project, not an optional extra.

**Multilingual design** — layouts and typographic systems that
function correctly in French, English, and other languages without
requiring separate design work per language. We design for the
longest string, the right-to-left edge case, and the screen reader
user simultaneously.

**Brand and visual identity** — identity systems for organisations
that need to communicate consistently across contexts without a
full-time design team. We deliver systems, not artefacts.

## Our approach

Good design is invisible to the person it serves. Our goal is never to
produce work that announces itself as design. It is to produce work
that allows the person using it to do what they came to do.

Reproducible, auditable, sovereign systems — designed to be
understood, maintained, and owned by the people who depend on them.

We design and build infrastructure that organisations can own outright
— not in the legal sense only, but in the operational sense. Systems
they can understand, document, rebuild, and hand off without asking
permission from a vendor.

Our infrastructure practice covers the full stack from physical
hosting decisions through to deployment pipelines, monitoring, backup,
and the documentation that makes it all maintainable by a human being
at two in the morning.

## What we work on

**Deployment pipelines** — reproducible build and deployment systems
that treat infrastructure as code, version-controlled and auditable.
We prefer simple, composable tools over platforms that abstract away
operational understanding.

**Self-hosted services** — migration away from proprietary SaaS
platforms toward open, self-operated alternatives where this serves
the organisation's sovereignty and privacy commitments. We do not
advocate self-hosting for its own sake; we advocate it where it
materially improves an organisation's agency.

**Operational documentation** — runbooks, architecture diagrams, and
recovery procedures that reflect the actual system, not an idealised
version of it. Documentation is treated as a first-class deliverable,
not an afterthought.

**Resilience and recovery** — backup systems with tested restore
procedures, incident response planning, and the kind of redundancy
that matches the actual risk profile of the organisation rather than
the risk profile of a much larger one.

## Our approach

We work from first principles rather than from a preferred tool stack.
The right infrastructure for a community health clinic is not the
right infrastructure for a national media organisation. We size the
complexity of the solution to the operational capacity of the team
that will maintain it.

title: "Agency Design System — Accessible, Multilingual Design Infrastructure for a National NGO"
navTitle: "Agency Design System"
order: 2

A complete design system and component library for a national NGO
operating in four languages — built for accessibility from the ground
up, maintainable by a small internal team, and independent of any
proprietary design toolchain.

## Overview

A national non-governmental organisation with programmes across twelve
provinces needed a coherent visual identity and digital presence that
could be maintained by a team of three non-specialist staff, translated
into four languages without design degradation, and used confidently
by people with a wide range of disabilities and technical access
levels.

The brief was explicit on two points: the system had to work without a
subscription to any design tool, and it had to achieve WCAG 2.2 Level
AA conformance at every touchpoint.

## Approach

We audited the existing digital presence and identified the thirty
most frequently used interface patterns. From these we derived a
minimal design token system: twelve colours, four type sizes, three
spacing scales. Everything else is composed from these primitives.

The component library was built in plain HTML and CSS — no framework
dependency, no build step for basic use. Each component ships with its
accessibility annotations, keyboard interaction model, and a
plain-language description suitable for non-technical staff.
Translations are managed through a simple key-value file per language,
requiring no design changes to switch languages.

We ran usability testing with twelve participants across three
disability categories and three levels of digital literacy before
finalising the system.

## Outcome

The NGO's digital presence is now consistent across all twelve
provincial sites. The internal team has shipped four major content
updates and one new programme page without external support. Automated
accessibility testing passes at 100% on all core pages. The French,
Cree, Inuktitut, and English versions are maintained in parallel by a
single content coordinator.

## What we built

- Design token system (colour, type, spacing)
- 30-component HTML/CSS library with full accessibility annotations
- Translation infrastructure (key-value i18n, no framework required)
- WCAG 2.2 Level AA conformance audit and remediation
- Staff training materials and maintenance guide
- Ongoing quarterly accessibility review process

38	slower or less reliable connections than the one this was built on.
39	
40	## Sovereignty
41	
42	You shouldn't have to trust our word that you could leave if you needed
43	to — you should be able to check. Every page of this site is a plain
44	text file, in an open format, tracked in version control. If the tools
45	we build with disappeared tomorrow, the content wouldn't disappear with
46	them.
47	
48	## Data Portability
49	
50	Closely tied to sovereignty, and worth naming on its own: nothing here
51	is locked behind a proprietary export process. What's readable by a
52	program is also readable by a person — a technically complete export
53	that only a developer can open isn't the same guarantee as one anyone
54	can.
55	
56	## Longevity
57	
58	We can't promise any particular tool we use today will still exist in
59	ten years — nobody honestly can. What we can commit to is choosing
60	plain, open formats and widely-used, forkable tools over proprietary or
61	fashionable ones, specifically so that the content outlives whatever
62	we're currently using to build it.

89	We are a studio of practitioners in technology, design, and
90	infrastructure — working with individuals and organisations who want
91	to operate with greater agency.
92	
93	## Who we are
94	
95	Vishpala is a multidisciplinary studio. We are technologists,
96	designers, and infrastructure specialists who work together on
97	problems that require all three disciplines to solve well.
98	
99	We take our name from the Rigvedic figure Vishpala — a warrior who
100	loses a leg in battle and is given an iron prosthetic by the Ashvins
101	so she can return to the field. We are interested in the idea of
102	prosthetics: tools and infrastructure that extend capability, restore
103	agency, and allow people to do what they came to do.
104	
105	## What we believe
106	
107	**Sovereignty matters.** Organisations that depend entirely on
108	infrastructure they do not control are fragile in ways that are not
109	always visible until something breaks. We help organisations
110	understand their dependencies and, where it serves them, reduce them.
111	
112	**Accessibility is not optional.** We do not build things that exclude
113	people with disabilities, and we do not help other organisations build
114	them. WCAG 2.2 Level AA is the floor we hold our own client work to.
115	
116	**Complexity should be proportionate.** The right infrastructure for a
117	community organisation is not the right infrastructure for a national
118	one. We size solutions to the actual operational capacity of the
119	people who will maintain them.
120	
121	**Excellence takes time.** We work on fewer things at once than most
122	studios. We do not take on work we cannot do well.
123	
124	## How we work
125	
126	We work in close collaboration with our clients throughout a project —
127	not in isolation with periodic check-ins. We believe the people who
128	will use and maintain what we build should understand it, which means
129	building understanding as we go rather than handing over a finished
130	system at the end.
131	
132	We work in English and French.

156	
157	## Commitment
158	
159	Accessibility is the first of our [commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/),
160	because everything else this site does depends on it. We treat it as a
161	core discipline of our practice, not a compliance exercise bolted on
162	at the end.
163	
164	## Current measures
165	
166	This site has been designed and built with accessibility as a primary
167	requirement. The following measures are in place:
168	
169	- Semantic HTML structure with appropriate landmark regions
170	- A "Skip to content" link as the first focusable element on every page
171	- Every interactive part of the site — the language switcher, the mobile menu, all navigation links — works from a keyboard alone, with visible focus outlines on every focusable element
172	- The mobile menu is a native `<details>`/`<summary>` disclosure rather than a custom JavaScript widget, so it behaves the way assistive technology already expects
173	- Nothing on this site depends on JavaScript to be readable or navigable
174	- Every page declares its own language (`lang="en"` or `lang="fr"`) and alternate-language links (`hreflang`)
175	- Where a page has no translation yet, the language switcher shows it as missing rather than linking somewhere broken
176	- Meaningful images carry descriptive alt text; decorative ones don't compete for a screen reader's attention
177	- Diagrams are plain SVG, not flattened screenshots, so their content stays selectable and scalable
178	- Text resizes fluidly with the browser's own zoom and font-size settings, rather than being fixed to a pixel size
179	- Fonts are self-hosted (see [Commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/)), so text still renders even when a third-party font host would otherwise block or slow the page
180	- Layout reflows for narrow screens and enlarged text without content being clipped or overlapping
181	
182	## Known limitations
183	
184	This statement describes intent and current practice, not a certified
185	audit or a claimed conformance level. If something on this site
186	doesn't work the way it's described here, that's a bug we want to
187	know about.
188	
189	No known issues at time of publication.

194	that prevents you from accessing content or using a feature — tell us
195	what page you were on and what happened:

199	We treat accessibility reports as a priority fix, not a backlog item.

289	
290	Our commitment to privacy as a foundational principle — not a
291	compliance exercise. For the minimal, factual account of what this
292	particular site collects, see the [Privacy Policy](/en-ca/about/legal/privacy/);
293	this page is about the principle behind it.
294	
295	## Principle
296	
297	Privacy at Vishpala is not a legal obligation we satisfy at minimum
298	cost. It is a foundational design principle that shapes every decision
299	about what we build, what data we collect, and what infrastructure we
300	use.
301	
302	We apply the seven foundational principles of Privacy by Design as
303	articulated by Ann Cavoukian:
304	
305	- Proactive, not reactive — preventive, not remedial
306	- Privacy as the default setting
307	- Privacy embedded into design
308	- Full functionality — positive-sum, not zero-sum
309	- End-to-end security — full lifecycle protection
310	- Visibility and transparency
311	- Respect for user privacy — keep it user-centric
312	
313	## What we collect and why
314	
315	**This website** — we do not use analytics tracking. We do not set
316	cookies. We do not load third-party scripts. No data about visitors to
317	this site is collected, transmitted to third parties, or retained.
318	
319	**Client engagements** — we collect the information necessary to
320	deliver our work: contact information, project materials, and
321	communications. We do not collect information beyond what is needed.
322	We do not retain client data beyond the period required for the
323	engagement and any applicable legal retention requirement.
324	
325	**Communications** — email and other communications with us are
326	stored on infrastructure we operate. We do not use email marketing
327	platforms or CRM systems that transmit your contact information to
328	third parties.
329	
330	## Your rights
331	
332	Under the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
333	(PIPEDA) and applicable provincial privacy legislation, you have the
334	right to:
335	
336	- Know what personal information we hold about you
337	- Access that information
338	- Request correction of inaccurate information
339	- Withdraw consent for processing where consent is the legal basis
340	- Have your information deleted, subject to legal retention requirements
341	
342	To exercise any of these rights, contact us at privacy@vishpala.com.
343	
344	## Infrastructure
345	
346	Our fonts are self-hosted — no request to Google Fonts or any other
347	third party just to render text. See [Commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/)
348	for the rest of what that principle covers on this site.
349	
350	## Contact
351	
352	Questions about this policy or about how we handle personal
353	information: privacy@vishpala.com.

364	
365	Our commitment to environmental and operational sustainability in the
366	work we do and how we do it.
367	
368	## Principle
369	
370	We build things that are meant to last. That commitment extends beyond
371	the technical quality of the work to its environmental and operational
372	footprint.
373	
374	Sustainability at Vishpala means building systems that consume the
375	minimum necessary resources, that can be maintained by small teams
376	without specialised infrastructure, and that do not accumulate
377	complexity faster than the capacity to understand and operate them.
378	
379	## Digital sustainability
380	
381	**Efficient infrastructure** — we design systems sized to actual
382	workload. We do not recommend infrastructure at a scale that requires
383	constant management overhead to justify its cost or complexity.
384	Smaller, simpler, better-understood systems are almost always more
385	sustainable than large, complex ones.
386	
387	**Minimal dependencies** — every dependency is a liability: a thing
388	that must be updated, monitored, and eventually replaced. We minimise
389	dependencies as a matter of practice, preferring solutions that
390	compose well from smaller, stable components over solutions that
391	introduce large dependency trees.
392	
393	**Long-lived software** — we prefer technologies with long track
394	records and stable interfaces over technologies that require frequent
395	rewrites to remain current. The most sustainable software is software
396	that does not need to be replaced.
397	
398	**No unnecessary data collection** — collecting data has an energy
399	cost. Storing data has an energy cost. Transmitting data has an energy
400	cost. We do not collect, store, or transmit data that does not serve a
401	clear purpose.
402	
403	## Operational sustainability
404	
405	**Documentation** — undocumented systems are unsustainable systems.
406	They accumulate technical debt invisibly and become dependent on the
407	continued availability of the people who built them. We treat
408	documentation as a core deliverable.
409	
410	**Knowledge transfer** — we build with the intention that our clients
411	can operate, maintain, and extend what we build without us. Dependency
412	on an external consultant is not a sustainable operational model.
413	
414	**Workload** — we do not take on more work than we can do well.
415	Overextended practitioners produce lower quality work and burn out. We
416	maintain a sustainable pace as a matter of professional principle.
417	
418	## What we do not yet do
419	
420	We do not currently measure or report the specific energy consumption
421	of the infrastructure we operate or recommend. This is a gap we intend
422	to address. We will update this commitment when we have a methodology
423	we are confident in.

444	
445	Conformance, remediation, and the organisational practice of building
446	things that work for everyone.
447	
448	Accessibility is not a checklist or a compliance exercise. It is the
449	practice of building things that work for the full range of people who
450	need to use them — across abilities, devices, languages, and connection
451	speeds.
452	
453	We approach accessibility as a discipline that runs through every stage
454	of a project, not a phase that happens after design and development are
455	complete. The cost of retrofitting accessibility is always higher than
456	building it in from the start.
457	
458	## What we work on
459	
460	**Conformance audits** — systematic evaluation of digital products
461	against WCAG 2.2 criteria, delivered as a prioritised remediation plan
462	with clear ownership and testable acceptance criteria. We audit to AA
463	as standard and AAA where the use case warrants it.
464	
465	**Remediation** — hands-on remediation of accessibility issues in
466	HTML, CSS, and content, including complex cases involving dynamic
467	content, single-page applications, and custom interactive components.
468	
469	**Procurement support** — accessibility requirements for RFPs and
470	vendor evaluation criteria, including evaluation of VPAT documentation
471	and independent testing of vendor claims.
472	
473	**Organisational practice** — training, process integration, and
474	tooling recommendations that build accessibility competence into a
475	team's standard workflow rather than concentrating it in a single
476	specialist.
477	
478	**Usability testing** — moderated testing sessions with participants
479	who use assistive technologies, screen readers, switch access, voice
480	control, and other access methods, delivering qualitative findings
481	that automated tools cannot surface.
482	
483	## Our approach
484	
485	Automated testing catches approximately 30% of accessibility issues.
486	The rest require human judgment. We combine automated scanning with
487	manual expert review and user testing because no single method is
488	sufficient on its own.

499	
500	Accessible, multilingual design systems built to serve people — not to
501	impress peers or satisfy platform requirements.
502	
503	We practice design as a discipline of clarity. Our work begins with the
504	people who will use it — their actual contexts, access levels,
505	languages, and needs — and builds outward from there toward visual
506	form, not the other way around.
507	
508	Design at Vishpala is inseparable from accessibility. We treat WCAG 2.2
509	Level AA conformance as a floor, not a ceiling, and we test with real
510	people across a range of abilities and assistive technologies at every
511	stage of a project.
512	
513	## What we work on
514	
515	**Design systems** — token-based, component-level design
516	infrastructure that can be maintained by a small team, translated
517	without visual degradation, and extended without breaking existing
518	patterns. We build for longevity, not for the current sprint.
519	
520	**Accessible interfaces** — visual design, interaction design, and
521	content design that work for people with a wide range of visual,
522	motor, cognitive, and linguistic access needs. We conduct usability
523	testing as a standard part of every project, not an optional extra.
524	
525	**Multilingual design** — layouts and typographic systems that
526	function correctly in French, English, and other languages without
527	requiring separate design work per language. We design for the
528	longest string, the right-to-left edge case, and the screen reader
529	user simultaneously.
530	
531	**Brand and visual identity** — identity systems for organisations
532	that need to communicate consistently across contexts without a
533	full-time design team. We deliver systems, not artefacts.
534	
535	## Our approach
536	
537	Good design is invisible to the person it serves. Our goal is never to
538	produce work that announces itself as design. It is to produce work
539	that allows the person using it to do what they came to do.

576	
577	Reproducible, auditable, sovereign systems — designed to be
578	understood, maintained, and owned by the people who depend on them.
579	
580	We design and build infrastructure that organisations can own outright
581	— not in the legal sense only, but in the operational sense. Systems
582	they can understand, document, rebuild, and hand off without asking
583	permission from a vendor.
584	
585	Our infrastructure practice covers the full stack from physical
586	hosting decisions through to deployment pipelines, monitoring, backup,
587	and the documentation that makes it all maintainable by a human being
588	at two in the morning.
589	
590	## What we work on
591	
592	**Deployment pipelines** — reproducible build and deployment systems
593	that treat infrastructure as code, version-controlled and auditable.
594	We prefer simple, composable tools over platforms that abstract away
595	operational understanding.
596	
597	**Self-hosted services** — migration away from proprietary SaaS
598	platforms toward open, self-operated alternatives where this serves
599	the organisation's sovereignty and privacy commitments. We do not
600	advocate self-hosting for its own sake; we advocate it where it
601	materially improves an organisation's agency.
602	
603	**Operational documentation** — runbooks, architecture diagrams, and
604	recovery procedures that reflect the actual system, not an idealised
605	version of it. Documentation is treated as a first-class deliverable,
606	not an afterthought.
607	
608	**Resilience and recovery** — backup systems with tested restore
609	procedures, incident response planning, and the kind of redundancy
610	that matches the actual risk profile of the organisation rather than
611	the risk profile of a much larger one.
612	
613	## Our approach
614	
615	We work from first principles rather than from a preferred tool stack.
616	The right infrastructure for a community health clinic is not the
617	right infrastructure for a national media organisation. We size the
618	complexity of the solution to the operational capacity of the team
619	that will maintain it.

672	
673	A complete design system and component library for a national NGO
674	operating in four languages — built for accessibility from the ground
675	up, maintainable by a small internal team, and independent of any
676	proprietary design toolchain.
677	
678	## Overview
679	
680	A national non-governmental organisation with programmes across twelve
681	provinces needed a coherent visual identity and digital presence that
682	could be maintained by a team of three non-specialist staff, translated
683	into four languages without design degradation, and used confidently
684	by people with a wide range of disabilities and technical access
685	levels.
686	
687	The brief was explicit on two points: the system had to work without a
688	subscription to any design tool, and it had to achieve WCAG 2.2 Level
689	AA conformance at every touchpoint.
690	
691	## Approach
692	
693	We audited the existing digital presence and identified the thirty
694	most frequently used interface patterns. From these we derived a
695	minimal design token system: twelve colours, four type sizes, three
696	spacing scales. Everything else is composed from these primitives.
697	
698	The component library was built in plain HTML and CSS — no framework
699	dependency, no build step for basic use. Each component ships with its
700	accessibility annotations, keyboard interaction model, and a
701	plain-language description suitable for non-technical staff.
702	Translations are managed through a simple key-value file per language,
703	requiring no design changes to switch languages.
704	
705	We ran usability testing with twelve participants across three
706	disability categories and three levels of digital literacy before
707	finalising the system.
708	
709	## Outcome
710	
711	The NGO's digital presence is now consistent across all twelve
712	provincial sites. The internal team has shipped four major content
713	updates and one new programme page without external support. Automated
714	accessibility testing passes at 100% on all core pages. The French,
715	Cree, Inuktitut, and English versions are maintained in parallel by a
716	single content coordinator.
717	
718	## What we built
719	
720	- Design token system (colour, type, spacing)
721	- 30-component HTML/CSS library with full accessibility annotations
722	- Translation infrastructure (key-value i18n, no framework required)
723	- WCAG 2.2 Level AA conformance audit and remediation
724	- Staff training materials and maintenance guide
725	- Ongoing quarterly accessibility review process

766	
767	A full infrastructure pivot away from proprietary cloud lock-in for a
768	regional health network serving 80,000 patients — replacing
769	vendor-managed services with reproducible, self-hosted, auditable
770	systems under the organisation's own operational control.
771	
772	## Overview
773	
774	A regional health network operating across six sites had accumulated
775	deep dependencies on three separate proprietary cloud platforms over
776	eight years of growth. The infrastructure was functional but opaque:
777	no single person understood the full system, vendor contracts were
778	auto-renewing without review, and patient data was processed across
779	jurisdictions in ways that were inconsistent with the organisation's
780	own privacy commitments.
781	
782	We were brought in to design and implement a path to operational
783	independence — one that did not require a "big bang" cutover and did
784	not introduce new categories of fragility in the process of removing
785	old ones.
786	
787	## Approach
788	
789	We began with a full infrastructure audit: every service, every data
790	flow, every external dependency mapped and documented. From that
791	baseline we identified three categories of dependency — those that
792	could be eliminated immediately, those requiring phased migration, and
793	those where a sovereign alternative did not yet exist and would need
794	to be built.
795	
796	The migration ran over fourteen months across four phases. We
797	prioritised patient data first, moving all clinical records to a
798	self-hosted, jurisdiction-compliant system with automated backup
799	verification and a tested restore procedure. We replaced the
800	vendor-managed identity system with an open, auditable alternative. We
801	decommissioned two SaaS platforms entirely by consolidating their
802	functions into tools the organisation already operated.
803	
804	## Outcome
805	
806	The network now operates a fully documented, reproducible
807	infrastructure. Every service can be rebuilt from version-controlled
808	configuration. The on-call team can understand the full system in a
809	single working day. Annual vendor contract costs were reduced by 68%.
810	The organisation's privacy commitments and its actual infrastructure
811	are now consistent with each other.
812	
813	## What we built
814	
815	- Full infrastructure audit and dependency map
816	- Phased migration plan with rollback procedures at each stage
817	- Self-hosted clinical records system with automated backup and restore testing
818	- Open identity and access management platform
819	- Runbooks and operational documentation for the internal team
820	- Training programme for three tiers of operational staff

823	title: "Accessibility Procurement Checklist — What to Ask Before You Buy"
824	navTitle: "Accessibility Procurement Checklist"
825	order: 3
826	identifier: "urn:uuid:cf9fe491-a757-4118-bdb6-6a1b7d005968"
827	relation: "urn:uuid:5ac1ea1b-9000-4cbb-9a6d-ac7749fc7625"
828	description: "A checklist for evaluating accessibility claims during software procurement — covering VPAT review, independent testing, contractual commitments, and what to do when a vendor cannot answer your questions."

830	---
831	
832	A checklist for evaluating accessibility claims during software
833	procurement — covering VPAT review, independent testing, contractual
834	commitments, and what to do when a vendor cannot answer your
835	questions.
836	
837	## Purpose
838	
839	Most software vendors will tell you their product is accessible. This
840	checklist helps you evaluate that claim before you sign a contract,
841	not after you have committed to a platform your users cannot use.
842	
843	## 1. Ask for the VPAT
844	
845	A Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT) is a vendor's
846	self-reported assessment of how their product conforms to
847	accessibility standards. Ask for the VPAT for the specific version of
848	the product you are evaluating, against WCAG 2.2 Level AA.
849	
850	Red flags in a VPAT:
851	
852	- It references WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 rather than 2.2
853	- Every criterion is listed as "Supports" with no explanation
854	- The evaluation was conducted by the vendor itself with no independent review
855	- It covers a version of the product that is more than one major release old
856	
857	## 2. Test independently
858	
859	Do not rely on the VPAT alone. Conduct or commission independent
860	testing before purchase. At minimum:
861	
862	- Run an automated scan using a current tool (Axe, WAVE, or equivalent)
863	- Navigate the core user flows using only a keyboard
864	- Test with a screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS)
865	- Check colour contrast on all text and interactive elements
866	
867	## 3. Ask contractual questions
868	
869	Before signing, ask:
870	
871	- What is the vendor's published accessibility conformance target?
872	- What is the process for reporting accessibility issues?
873	- What is the committed remediation timeframe for critical accessibility barriers?
874	- Are accessibility commitments included in the SLA?
875	
876	A vendor who cannot answer these questions is a vendor who has not
877	made accessibility a priority. That is useful information.
878	
879	## 4. When a vendor cannot meet your requirements
880	
881	If a vendor cannot demonstrate conformance and will not make
882	contractual commitments, you have three options: require conformance
883	as a condition of contract, require a remediation plan with milestones
884	as a condition of contract, or choose a different vendor.
885	
886	Accepting an inaccessible product because it meets other requirements
887	is a decision that excludes some of your users. That decision should
888	be made explicitly and documented, not absorbed quietly into a
889	procurement process.

900	
901	A plain-language introduction to design tokens: what they are, why
902	they matter for multilingual and accessible design, and how to
903	implement a minimal token system without a design tool subscription.
904	
905	## What is a design token?
906	
907	A design token is a named value that encodes a design decision.
908	Instead of writing `color: #0033cc` in five hundred places, you define
909	a token — `--colour-primary: #0033cc` — and reference the token
910	everywhere. When the decision changes, you change it in one place.
911	
912	Tokens are the infrastructure layer of a design system. They are not a
913	design tool feature or a framework requirement. They are CSS custom
914	properties, and they work in any browser.
915	
916	## Why tokens matter for accessible, multilingual design
917	
918	**Accessibility** — tokens make it tractable to verify colour contrast
919	across an entire system. If your text colour and background colour are
920	both tokens, you can check every combination in one place rather than
921	hunting through a codebase for hardcoded values.
922	
923	**Multilingual design** — tokens make it straightforward to adjust
924	typographic decisions for specific languages. A French interface may
925	need slightly more generous line height than an English one. A
926	token-based system lets you override a single value per language
927	rather than rewriting layout rules.
928	
929	**Maintainability** — a small team can maintain a token-based system
930	because changes are localised. Replacing the primary colour takes two
931	minutes, not two days.
932	
933	## A minimal token system
934	
935	A minimal token system for a small organisation typically needs four
936	categories:
937	
938	- **Colour** — three to five colours maximum. A primary colour, a text colour, a background colour, a border colour, and one semantic colour (for errors or warnings if needed). Every other colour in the system should be derived from these or be black or white.
939	- **Typography** — two to three font sizes for body text, one or two for headings, and one for small labels. A line height for each. A font stack per typeface used.
940	- **Spacing** — four to six spacing values on a consistent scale, e.g. 0.25rem, 0.5rem, 1rem, 2rem, 4rem. Everything else is composed from these.
941	- **Layout** — a maximum content width and a standard gap value for grid layouts.
942	
943	## Implementation
944	
945	```css
946	:root {
947	  --colour-primary: #0033cc;
948	  --colour-text: #000000;
949	  --colour-background: #ffffff;
950	  --colour-border: #d0d0d0;
951	  --font-body: system-ui, sans-serif;
952	  --size-sm: 0.875rem;
953	  --size-base: 1rem;
954	  --size-lg: 1.25rem;
955	  --size-xl: 1.75rem;
956	  --space-sm: 0.5rem;
957	  --space-md: 1rem;
958	  --space-lg: 2rem;
959	  --space-xl: 4rem;
960	  --measure: 70ch;
961	}
962	```
963	
964	That's a complete minimal token system. Everything else is
965	composition.

992	identifier: "urn:uuid:2c87d848-fc95-4690-934f-379292d5f582"
993	relation: "urn:uuid:b11022df-d208-4fb2-9f19-27e4677cab01"
994	description: "A practical guide to conducting a full infrastructure audit: what to document, how to surface hidden dependencies, and how to produce a map that is actually useful for decision-making."

996	---
997	
998	A practical guide to conducting a full infrastructure audit: what to
999	document, how to surface hidden dependencies, and how to produce a map
1000	that is actually useful for decision-making.
1001	
1002	## Purpose
1003	
1004	Before any infrastructure work begins, you need an accurate picture of
1005	what exists. This guide describes how to conduct a full infrastructure
1006	audit — not a theoretical inventory, but a working document that
1007	reflects the system as it actually operates.
1008	
1009	## 1. What to capture
1010	
1011	A useful infrastructure audit captures six categories of information:
1012	
1013	- **Services** — every running service, its purpose, its operator, and its dependencies
1014	- **Data flows** — where data originates, where it is processed, where it is stored, and where it leaves your control
1015	- **Access and credentials** — who has access to what, under what authentication model, and where credentials are stored
1016	- **External dependencies** — every third-party service, API, or platform the system depends on
1017	- **Contracts and costs** — every vendor contract, its renewal date, its cost, and what it would take to exit it
1018	- **Documentation** — what documentation exists, how current it is, and where it lives
1019	
1020	## 2. How to surface hidden dependencies
1021	
1022	Hidden dependencies are the most dangerous part of any infrastructure.
1023	They are things the system depends on that nobody has explicitly
1024	decided to depend on — accumulated through years of pragmatic
1025	decisions that were never revisited.
1026	
1027	Common sources of hidden dependencies include:
1028	
1029	- DNS records pointing to services that no longer exist but whose removal would break something
1030	- Email delivery relying on a personal account held by a former employee
1031	- Authentication flows that pass through a third-party service inserted years ago as a temporary measure
1032	- Backup jobs that write to a location that has quietly run out of space
1033	- SSL certificates managed by a person who has left the organisation
1034	
1035	The most reliable way to surface hidden dependencies is to map data
1036	flows from the outside in: start from every public-facing URL and
1037	follow each request through the system until it reaches persistent
1038	storage or exits to a third party.
1039	
1040	## 3. Producing a useful map
1041	
1042	An infrastructure map is only useful if it reflects the actual system
1043	and can be read by someone who did not build it. It should include:
1044	
1045	- A diagram showing major components and the connections between them
1046	- A table of services with owner, dependencies, and last-verified date
1047	- A list of external dependencies with contract and cost information
1048	- A list of open questions that the audit surfaced but could not resolve
1049	
1050	The map should be version-controlled alongside the infrastructure it
1051	describes and updated whenever a significant change is made.

1054	title: "Self-Hosting Decision Framework — When to Run It Yourself and When Not To"
1055	navTitle: "Self-Hosting Decision Framework"
1056	order: 4
1057	identifier: "urn:uuid:7f538f3d-ea81-446c-ae61-94a99bbb5a0f"
1058	relation: "urn:uuid:2428f521-d6fb-4493-9b62-e569e02ba7ab"
1059	description: "A practical framework for deciding when self-hosting a service improves your organisation's agency and when it introduces complexity without commensurate benefit."
1060	type: "Text"

1062	
1063	A practical framework for deciding when self-hosting a service
1064	improves your organisation's agency and when it introduces complexity
1065	without commensurate benefit.
1066	
1067	## Purpose
1068	
1069	Self-hosting is not inherently better than using a managed service.
1070	The question is always whether self-hosting, for this service, for
1071	this organisation, at this moment, produces a better outcome than the
1072	available alternatives. This framework helps structure that decision.
1073	
1074	## 1. The four questions
1075	
1076	Before deciding to self-host any service, answer four questions:
1077	
1078	1. **What do you gain?** Enumerate the specific benefits: data
1079	   sovereignty, reduced cost, elimination of a vendor dependency,
1080	   alignment with a privacy commitment, the ability to customise
1081	   behaviour the vendor will not support. Be concrete. "More control"
1082	   is not sufficient — control over what, specifically?
1083	2. **What does it cost to operate?** Self-hosted services require
1084	   someone to maintain them: applying security updates, monitoring for
1085	   failures, managing backups, and responding when things break. Who
1086	   will do this? What is their capacity? What happens when they are
1087	   unavailable?
1088	3. **What is the failure mode?** If the self-hosted service fails,
1089	   what is the impact? How quickly can it be restored? Is there a
1090	   tested recovery procedure? The failure mode of a self-hosted
1091	   service is typically your problem to solve in a way that a managed
1092	   service's failure mode is not.
1093	4. **What is the exit cost?** If self-hosting turns out to be the
1094	   wrong decision, how much effort does it take to migrate to a
1095	   managed service? Low exit cost makes the decision reversible. High
1096	   exit cost means you need to be more confident before you commit.
1097	
1098	## 2. When self-hosting is clearly the right choice
1099	
1100	Self-hosting is clearly the right choice when:
1101	
1102	- The data processed by the service is sensitive and subject to jurisdiction requirements that managed services cannot satisfy
1103	- The organisation has the operational capacity to maintain the service reliably
1104	- The managed alternatives are prohibitively expensive relative to the value delivered
1105	- The managed alternatives have unacceptable lock-in characteristics
1106	
1107	## 3. When managed services are clearly the right choice
1108	
1109	Managed services are clearly the right choice when:
1110	
1111	- The operational cost of self-hosting exceeds the cost of the managed service
1112	- The organisation does not have the capacity to respond to failures reliably
1113	- The service is not part of the organisation's core operational competence
1114	- The data processed is not sensitive and jurisdiction is not a concern
1115	
1116	## 4. The honest answer most of the time
1117	
1118	Most organisations should self-host fewer things than idealists
1119	advocate and more things than vendors prefer. The right answer depends
1120	entirely on operational capacity, data sensitivity, and the specific
1121	alternatives available. Anyone who gives you a blanket answer is not
1122	engaging with your actual situation.

1133	
1134	How vishpala.com approaches typography: system-ui as the default, with
1135	Atkinson Hyperlegible available as a user-selectable accessible
1136	alternative, self-hosted with no external dependencies.
1137	
1138	## The approach
1139	
1140	This site uses `system-ui, sans-serif` — the device's native font
1141	stack — as its default typography. No fonts are loaded from external
1142	sources. As a user-selectable alternative, Atkinson Hyperlegible is
1143	available and self-hosted: all font files are served directly from
1144	this site with no third-party requests.
1145	
1146	## System-ui — the default
1147	
1148	System fonts are the typefaces operating system vendors have spent the
1149	most resources optimising for screen legibility at every size, display
1150	density, and accessibility setting. San Francisco on macOS and iOS,
1151	Segoe UI on Windows, and Roboto on Android are each the product of
1152	significant investment in hinting, spacing, and rendering.
1153	
1154	System fonts respond correctly to the user's own font preferences. If
1155	a user has configured their operating system to use a larger default
1156	font size or a specific typeface for readability reasons, system-ui
1157	inherits those preferences. For users who depend on those preferences,
1158	that inheritance is important.
1159	
1160	`system-ui` introduces no external dependency of any kind and imposes
1161	no infrastructure maintenance burden.
1162	
1163	## Atkinson Hyperlegible — the accessible alternative
1164	
1165	Atkinson Hyperlegible was designed by the Braille Institute
1166	specifically for readers with low vision. Each character is uniquely
1167	formed to prevent misreading — the letterforms for commonly confused
1168	pairs (1/l/I, 0/O, rn/m) are deliberately differentiated. The Braille
1169	Institute released it under the SIL Open Font Licence 1.1, permitting
1170	free use and redistribution.
1171	
1172	The Inclusive Design Research Centre at OCAD University documents
1173	Atkinson Hyperlegible as a recommended typeface for low-vision
1174	accessibility.
1175	
1176	## Sovereignty and performance
1177	
1178	Neither typography option loads fonts from Google Fonts or any other
1179	external source. There is no connection to a third-party font delivery
1180	network and no disclosure of visitor IP addresses to font providers.
1181	
1182	When system-ui is active, text renders immediately using a font
1183	already present on the device — no network request, no flash of
1184	invisible text, no layout shift.

# Sveltia CMS config (Decap-compatible format).
#
# backend.name is github, matching this repo — NOT a placeholder to
# swap later. Sveltia CMS dropped Git Gateway support entirely (not
# just discouraged — genuinely unimplemented, confirmed directly
# against Sveltia's own docs: "Bitbucket, Gitea/Forgejo and Git Gateway
# backends will not be supported due to performance limitations"), so
# `git-gateway` here wasn't a deferred config choice, it was a config
# that could never have worked. Supported backends as of writing:
# github, gitlab, gitea (self-hosted Gitea/Forgejo), test (an in-memory
# backend for trying the CMS without touching real files).
#
# For LOCAL testing without setting up GitHub OAuth: Sveltia's Local
# Development Workflow lets you skip auth entirely — run the dev
# server, open /admin/index.html in Chrome or Edge, and click "Work
# with Local Repository" to grant File System Access API permission on
# this project's root folder directly. No proxy server, no OAuth app,
# no local_backend config flag needed (that's the old Decap mechanism;
# Sveltia replaced it with this). Real remote access (from anywhere,
# not just this machine) does need OAuth — either Sveltia's own
# Authenticator (deployable to Cloudflare Workers) or a personal access
# token; not configured here, since it's not needed for local
# verification of the fixes in this file.
backend:
  name: github
  repo: steelcj/vishpala-eleventy-mvp
  branch: main

site_url: https://vishpala.com
logo_url: /assets/img/logos/logo-lockup-dark.svg

# Per-entry relative media: with an empty collection-level media_folder,
# Sveltia/Decap resolve a field's relative media_folder against the entry
# being edited, so an image field with media_folder: "index.assets" lands
# beside that entry's own index.md. Verify this against Sveltia's current
# docs before relying on it in production — media-folder resolution rules
# have shifted between CMS versions.
media_folder: ""
public_folder: ""

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# File Collections model (migrated from Folder Collections).
#
# WHY: Sveltia CMS cannot create new nested folders through its UI —
# confirmed directly from the maintainer (github.com/sveltia/sveltia-cms
# discussions #598): "a non-dev user wouldn't be able to create a new
# folder in the sidebar... one of our unimplemented features... it will
# be added to Sveltia CMS 2.0." The old Folder Collections
# (path: "{{slug}}/index") could never reach two-level-deep pages like
# about/commitments/index.md or about/legal/privacy.md — those pages
# only existed because they were hand-placed outside the CMS. See
# docs/swot--how-sveltia-cms-should-model-translation-and-page-structure.md
# for the full analysis (including why native i18n doesn't solve this
# either — this site's translated URL slugs, about/a-propos etc., can't
# be expressed through the {{locale}} placeholder).
#
# WHAT CHANGES FOR EDITORS: every page below can be opened and edited
# freely from the CMS sidebar. A genuinely NEW page — one that doesn't
# exist yet — still requires a developer to add a `files:` entry here
# first. That's a disclosed, real limitation of Sveltia CMS today, not
# a workaround failure. Revisit if Sveltia ships nested collections
# (2.0, not yet released as of the "Currency check" in the SWOT doc
# above) — check that doc's "Currency check" section before assuming
# this constraint still holds; this project ships frequently.
#
# WHAT DIDN'T CHANGE: the actual content/ file tree. Every path below
# is identical to where these files already lived — only the CMS's
# description of them changed.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

"""Write the es-ca Expressions of every Work that exists in both en-ca and fr-ca.

Run with the site root as the only argument. Each page gets a fresh
urn:uuid identifier (random, version 4, as `uuidgen -r` makes) and the
same relation UUID as its en-ca and fr-ca counterparts. Refuses to
overwrite an existing file.
"""
import json
import sys
import uuid
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(sys.argv[1]) / "content" / "es-ca"


def q(value):
    return json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False)


def page(path, fm, body):
    target = ROOT / path
    if target.exists():
        raise SystemExit(f"refusing to overwrite {target}")
    lines = ["---"]
    for key in ("title", "navTitle", "order"):
        if key in fm:
            v = fm[key]
            lines.append(f"{key}: {v if isinstance(v, int) else q(v)}")
    lines.append(f'identifier: "urn:uuid:{uuid.uuid4()}"')
    lines.append(f'relation: "{fm["relation"]}"')
    for key in ("layout", "description", "coverage"):
        if key in fm:
            lines.append(f"{key}: {q(fm[key])}")
    lines.append('type: "Text"')
    for key in ("headerMenu", "footerMenu"):
        if key in fm:
            lines.append(f"{key}: {'true' if fm[key] else 'false'}")
    lines.append("---")
    text = "\n".join(lines) + "\n" + ("\n" + body.strip() + "\n" if body.strip() else "")
    target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    target.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
    print(target.relative_to(ROOT.parent.parent))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Home

page("proyectos/sovereign-stack.md", {
    "title": "Sovereign Stack — Independencia de infraestructura para una red regional de salud",
    "navTitle": "Sovereign Stack", "order": 1,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:f7670414-604a-4185-9121-f85e26f4f46f",
    "description": "Un cambio completo de infraestructura para salir de la dependencia de nubes propietarias en una red regional de salud que atiende a 80 000 pacientes, reemplazando servicios gestionados por proveedores con sistemas reproducibles, autoalojados y auditables bajo el control operativo de la propia organización.",
    "coverage": "Marzo de 2026, completado",
}, """
Un cambio completo de infraestructura para salir de la dependencia de
nubes propietarias en una red regional de salud que atiende a 80 000
pacientes, reemplazando servicios gestionados por proveedores con
sistemas reproducibles, autoalojados y auditables bajo el control
operativo de la propia organización.

## Panorama general

Una red regional de salud que opera en seis sedes había acumulado, en
ocho años de crecimiento, dependencias profundas de tres plataformas de
nube propietarias distintas. La infraestructura funcionaba, pero era
opaca: nadie entendía el sistema completo, los contratos con
proveedores se renovaban automáticamente sin revisión y los datos de
pacientes se procesaban en distintas jurisdicciones de maneras
incompatibles con los compromisos de privacidad de la propia
organización.

Nos llamaron para diseñar y poner en marcha un camino hacia la
independencia operativa: uno que no exigiera un cambio de golpe y que
no introdujera nuevas formas de fragilidad mientras se eliminaban las
antiguas.

## Enfoque

Empezamos con una auditoría completa de la infraestructura: cada
servicio, cada flujo de datos y cada dependencia externa, mapeados y
documentados. A partir de esa base identificamos tres categorías de
dependencias: las que se podían eliminar de inmediato, las que
requerían una migración por fases y aquellas para las que todavía no
existía una alternativa soberana y habría que construirla.

La migración duró catorce meses, en cuatro fases. Dimos prioridad a los
datos de pacientes: trasladamos todos los expedientes clínicos a un
sistema autoalojado y conforme a la jurisdicción, con verificación
automática de las copias de seguridad y un procedimiento de
restauración probado. Reemplazamos el sistema de identidad gestionado
por el proveedor con una alternativa abierta y auditable. Dimos de baja
por completo dos plataformas SaaS, consolidando sus funciones en
herramientas que la organización ya operaba.

## Resultado

Hoy la red opera una infraestructura totalmente documentada y
reproducible. Cada servicio se puede reconstruir a partir de una
configuración bajo control de versiones. El equipo de guardia puede
entender el sistema completo en una sola jornada de trabajo. El costo
anual de los contratos con proveedores se redujo un 68 %. Los
compromisos de privacidad de la organización y su infraestructura real
ahora son coherentes entre sí.

## Lo que construimos

- Auditoría completa de la infraestructura y mapa de dependencias
- Plan de migración por fases, con procedimientos de reversión en cada etapa
- Sistema autoalojado de expedientes clínicos, con copias de seguridad automáticas y pruebas de restauración
- Plataforma abierta de gestión de identidades y accesos
- Manuales de operación y documentación operativa para el equipo interno
- Programa de formación para tres niveles de personal operativo
""")

page("proyectos/agency-design-system.md", {
    "title": "Agency Design System — Infraestructura de diseño accesible y multilingüe para una ONG nacional",
    "navTitle": "Agency Design System", "order": 2,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:54debb25-b7b3-46e8-9bae-32cca1674d64",
    "description": "Un sistema de diseño y una biblioteca de componentes completos para una ONG nacional que trabaja en cuatro idiomas: accesible desde la base, mantenible por un pequeño equipo interno e independiente de cualquier herramienta de diseño propietaria.",
    "coverage": "Enero de 2026, completado",
}, """
Un sistema de diseño y una biblioteca de componentes completos para una
ONG nacional que trabaja en cuatro idiomas: accesible desde la base,
mantenible por un pequeño equipo interno e independiente de cualquier
herramienta de diseño propietaria.

## Panorama general

Una organización no gubernamental nacional, con programas en doce
provincias, necesitaba una identidad visual y una presencia digital
coherentes que pudiera mantener un equipo de tres personas no
especialistas, que pudieran traducirse a cuatro idiomas sin degradar el
diseño y que pudieran usar con confianza personas con una gran
diversidad de discapacidades y niveles de acceso a la tecnología.

El encargo era explícito en dos puntos: el sistema tenía que funcionar
sin suscripción a ninguna herramienta de diseño y tenía que cumplir el
nivel AA de las WCAG 2.2 en todos los puntos de contacto.

## Enfoque

Auditamos la presencia digital existente e identificamos los treinta
patrones de interfaz más usados. A partir de ellos definimos un sistema
mínimo de tokens de diseño: doce colores, cuatro tamaños de letra y
tres escalas de espaciado. Todo lo demás se compone a partir de estos
elementos básicos.

La biblioteca de componentes se construyó en HTML y CSS sencillos: sin
dependencia de ningún framework y sin paso de compilación para el uso
básico. Cada componente incluye sus anotaciones de accesibilidad, su
modelo de interacción con teclado y una descripción en lenguaje claro
pensada para personal no técnico. Las traducciones se gestionan con un
archivo sencillo de claves y valores por idioma, de modo que cambiar de
idioma no requiere ningún cambio de diseño.

Antes de cerrar el sistema hicimos pruebas de usabilidad con doce
participantes de tres categorías de discapacidad y tres niveles de
alfabetización digital.

## Resultado

La presencia digital de la ONG ahora es coherente en los doce sitios
provinciales. El equipo interno ha publicado cuatro actualizaciones
importantes de contenido y una nueva página de programa sin apoyo
externo. Las pruebas automáticas de accesibilidad pasan al 100 % en
todas las páginas principales. Las versiones en francés, cree,
inuktitut e inglés las mantiene en paralelo una sola persona
coordinadora de contenido.

## Lo que construimos

- Sistema de tokens de diseño (color, tipografía, espaciado)
- Biblioteca HTML/CSS de 30 componentes con anotaciones de accesibilidad completas
- Infraestructura de traducción (i18n con claves y valores, sin framework)
- Auditoría de conformidad con las WCAG 2.2 nivel AA y corrección de problemas
- Materiales de formación para el personal y guía de mantenimiento
- Proceso trimestral continuo de revisión de accesibilidad
""")
